All three pass every test here. Use bisect_right (first value <= target), not bisect_left: the target can be the first value of a row.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Check Every Cell Scan O(m·n) O(1) Ignores the sorting
Staircase from the Top-Right Drop a row or a column per step O(m + n) O(1) Also solves 240
Binary Search the Flattened Matrix Position p → (p // n, p % n) O(log(m·n)) O(1) Expected answer
153. Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array Medium Array Binary Search
Key idea: Binary search, comparing nums[mid] with nums[hi]. If nums[mid] > nums[hi], the drop (and the minimum) is to the right of mid: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise mid..hi is sorted and the minimum is mid or left of it: hi = mid. Stop when lo == hi. O(log n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

A sorted array of different numbers was rotated some number of times (moving the last number to the front each time), maybe zero times. Return the smallest number, in O(log n) time.

  • 1 <= n <= 5000
  • -5000 <= nums[i] <= 5000, all different

Example: [3,4,5,1,2] → 1. [4,5,6,7,0,1,2] → 0. [11,13,15,17] → 11 (not rotated).

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[3,1,2] 1 hi = mid - 1 throws away mid, which can be the minimum: said 3.
[2,1] 1 Looping on lo <= hi while setting hi = mid never ends: stuck here after 1,000 rounds.
[1,2,3,4] 1 Not rotated. Searching for "the first number smaller than nums[0]" without a separate check said 4. Comparing mid with nums[lo] instead of nums[hi] said 3.
[1] 1 One number: the loop doesn't run.
[2,3,4,5,1] 1 The minimum is last.
[5,1,2,3,4] 1 The minimum is second: the drop is right at the start.

Approach 1: Look at Every Number

Scan the array and keep the smallest number.

  • Always right, but ignores that the array is sorted.
  • Doesn't meet the O(log n) requirement.
Time O(n) Space O(1)

At n = 5000, averaged over 1,000 arrays: Python 70 µs, Java 3.5 µs, C++ 0.3 µs per call.

Approach 2: Binary Search Against nums[0]

If nums[0] <= nums[-1], the array isn't rotated: return nums[0]. Otherwise everything before the drop is ≥ nums[0] and everything after is smaller, so binary search for the first number smaller than nums[0].

  • A clear "yes/no" split, the kind binary search is built for.
  • The not-rotated check is required: there's no number smaller than nums[0] then.
Time O(log n) Space O(1)

At n = 5000: Python 13 µs, Java 0.6 µs, C++ 0.1 µs per call, 5× faster than the scan in Python. About 13 comparisons instead of 5000.

Approach 3: Binary Search Against nums[hi] Optimal

Compare nums[mid] with nums[hi]. Bigger: the array drops somewhere after mid, so lo = mid + 1. Smaller: mid..hi is sorted, so the minimum is mid or left of it, hi = mid. When one number is left, it's the minimum.

  • No special case: a not-rotated array just keeps moving hi left.
  • hi = mid with while lo < hi go together; mixing in mid - 1 or lo <= hi breaks it.
Time O(log n) Space O(1)

At n = 5000: Python 11 µs, Java 1.0 µs, C++ 0.15 µs per call. The expected answer. With duplicates allowed (problem 154), equal values need hi -= 1, and the worst case becomes O(n).

In practice Built-ins

min(nums) in Python, std::min_element in C++, Arrays.stream(nums).min() in Java. All scan the whole array.

Time O(n) Space O(1)

Python 70 µs, Java 19 µs, C++ 3.3 µs per call at n = 5000 here: fine for everyday code, but it's Approach 1, so it misses the point of the problem.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Look at Every Number Linear scan O(n) O(1) Ignores the order
Binary Search Against nums[0] First number smaller than nums[0] O(log n) O(1) Needs a not-rotated check
Binary Search Against nums[hi] Bigger than nums[hi]: go right O(log n) O(1) Expected answer
704. Binary Search Easy Binary Search Array
Key idea: Keep lo and hi so that target, if it's there, is always in nums[lo..hi]. Look at the middle: too small means drop it and everything to its left (lo = mid + 1); too big means drop it and everything to its right (hi = mid − 1). Loop while lo <= hi. O(log n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

nums is sorted in ascending order with no repeats. Return the index of target, or -1 if it isn't there. It must run in O(log n).

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10⁴, values in (-10⁴, 10⁴)

Example: [-1,0,3,5,9,12], target = 9 → 4. Same array, target = 2 → -1.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[5], target = 5 0 Looping while lo < hi skips the last remaining value: it said -1. Wrong on 1022 of 3008 tests.
[5], target = -5 -1 Setting hi = mid (not mid − 1) with lo <= hi never shrinks a 1-value range: it looped forever. Hit on 873 tests.
[2,5], target = 9 -1 Bigger than everything: lo walks off the right end and the loop stops.

Approach 1: Linear Scan

Check every value from the left. It ignores that the array is sorted, and doesn't meet the O(log n) rule.

Time O(n) Space O(1)

10⁴ values, target at the end: Python 233 µs, Java 22 µs, C++ 3.5 µs, about 100 times slower than binary search in Python.

Approach 2: Recursive Binary Search

find(lo, hi) compares target with nums[mid] and calls itself on the half that can still hold it. An empty range (lo > hi) means not found.

  • Clear to read; the calls are only about log₂ n = 14 deep for 10⁴ values.
  • mid = lo + (hi − lo) / 2 in C++ and Java avoids overflowing lo + hi on huge arrays.
Time O(log n) Space O(log n) call stack

10⁴ values, target at the end: Python 4.0 µs, Java 0.2 µs, C++ under 0.1 µs.

Approach 3: Iterative Binary Search Optimal

The same search as a loop: while lo <= hi, compare with the middle, then move lo or hi past it.

  • Every step drops mid itself, so the range always shrinks and the loop always ends.
Time O(log n) Space O(1)

10⁴ values, target at the end: Python 1.8 µs, Java 0.3 µs, C++ 0.3 µs. Too fast to tell apart from Approach 2 in C++ and Java.

In practice Built-ins

Python's bisect.bisect_left and C++'s std::lower_bound give the first index with a value ≥ target; check that it's equal. Java's Arrays.binarySearch returns a negative number when the value is missing.

Time O(log n) Space O(1)

Should pass on LeetCode. In Python, bisect took 1.5 µs, a little faster than the loop. Java's negative result encodes where the value would go, so turn it into −1.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Linear Scan Check every value O(n) O(1) Breaks the O(log n) rule
Recursive Binary Search Recurse into one half O(log n) O(log n) About 14 calls deep
Iterative Binary Search Move lo or hi past mid O(log n) O(1) Expected answer
Linked List 11 problems Pointer rewiring and dummy heads
2. Add Two Numbers Medium Linked List Math Recursion
Key idea: Digits are stored in reverse order, so the heads are the ones place. Walk both lists together like column addition: sum = a + b + carry, keep sum % 10, carry sum // 10. Use a dummy head node and keep looping while either list or the carry is left.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order, and each node holds a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list in the same format.

  • Each list has between 1 and 100 nodes.
  • Each node value is between 0 and 9.
  • No leading zeros, except for the number 0 itself.

Example: [2,4,3] + [5,6,4] is 342 + 465 = 807, so the answer is [7,0,8].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
l1 = [0], l2 = [0] [0] Both numbers are 0: the answer is one node, [0], not an empty list.
l1 = [5], l2 = [5] [0, 1] 5 + 5 = 10: the last carry needs a new node at the end.
l1 = [9,9,9,9,9,9,9], l2 = [9,9,9,9] [8, 9, 9, 9, 0, 0, 0, 1] Different lengths, a carry on every digit, and a final carry.
l1 = [9, 9], l2 = [1] [0, 0, 1] The shorter list ends but the carry keeps going through the longer one.
l1 = [1, 8], l2 = [0] [1, 8] Adding 0: the result is just the longer list.
l1 = 99 zeros then 1 (10⁹⁹), l2 = [1] [1, then 98 zeros, then 1] 100 digits: too big for int or long. Converting to a number only works with Python ints or Java's BigInteger.

Approach 1: Three Loops with Trailing Node

Handle the lists in three phases, writing the result digit by digit into a pre-allocated node.

  • Loop 1: while both lists have nodes, add l1.val + l2.val + carry.
  • Loop 2 and 3: whichever list is longer, keep going with val + carry.
  • If a carry of 1 is left, write it into one more node.
  • After every digit a new empty node is created, so the list ends with one extra node. Track prev and set prev.next = None at the end to cut it off.
Time O(max(m, n)) Space O(max(m, n))

Each node is visited once. The space is the output list itself, so there are no extra data structures. The downside is the repeated code across the three loops and the extra trailing node that has to be trimmed.

Approach 2: Single Loop with Dummy Head Optimal

Same column addition, but merge the three loops into one. Keep looping while l1, l2 or carry is still present, and treat a missing node as the digit 0.

  • Start with a dummy node and a tail pointer. Return dummy.next.
  • Each step: total = carry + (l1 digit) + (l2 digit), append a node with total % 10, set carry = total // 10.
  • Including carry in the loop condition handles the final carry (like 5 + 5 = 10) without a special case.
  • Nodes are only created when needed, so there's no trailing node to trim.
Time O(max(m, n)) Space O(max(m, n))

Same complexity as Approach 1 (the output list is the only space used, extra space is O(1)), but shorter, with no duplicated loops and no prev bookkeeping.

In practice Built-ins

Skip the column addition: turn each list into a real number, add them, and turn the sum back into a list. Python's int and Java's BigInteger handle numbers of any size, so 100-digit inputs are fine.

Time O(m + n) Space O(m + n)

Should pass on LeetCode. C++ has no built-in big integer (a long long overflows past 19 digits), so use Approach 2 there. The hidden cost is the string ↔ number conversions, which is fine at this size.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Three Loops with Trailing Node Both lists, then leftovers, then carry O(max(m, n)) O(max(m, n)) Works, but repeated code and a trailing node to trim
Single Loop with Dummy Head One loop; missing node or carry counts as 0 O(max(m, n)) O(max(m, n)) Cleaner, handles the final carry naturally
19. Remove Nth Node From End of List Medium Linked List Two Pointers
Key idea: Put a dummy node in front of the head, start fast and slow on it, and move fast n + 1 steps ahead. Then move both until fast is null: slow is now just before the node to remove, so slow.next = slow.next.next. Return dummy.next. One pass, O(1) space.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the head of a linked list, remove the n-th node from the end and return the head.

  • The list has between 1 and 30 nodes.
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 100 and 1 <= n <= length.
  • Follow-up: can you do it in one pass?

Examples: [1,2,3,4,5], n = 2 → [1,2,3,5]; [1], n = 1 → []; [1,2], n = 1 → [1].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1], n = 1 [] The only node goes: return null / None, not the old head.
[1,2], n = 2 [2] Removing the head: there's no node before it to update. A dummy node in front handles this without a special case.
[1,2,3,4,5], n = 5 [2,3,4,5] n equals the length: also the head. Without a dummy, moving fast n + 1 steps runs past the end.
[1,2], n = 1 [1] Removing the tail: the new last node must point to null.
[1,2,3,4,5], n = 2 [1,2,3,5] The usual case: off-by-one errors land on 3 or 5 instead of 4.
[1,1,1], n = 2 [1,1] Remove by position, not by value: comparing values can't tell these nodes apart.
30 nodes, n = 30 or n = 1 29 nodes The extremes at the largest size: the head and the tail.

Approach 1: Count the Length, Then Walk

The n-th from the end is the (length - n + 1)-th from the start. Count the nodes in a first pass, then walk to the node just before it and skip over it.

  • Start prev on a dummy node in front of the head and move it length - n times. When the target is the head, that's 0 moves and prev is the dummy.
  • prev.next = prev.next.next removes it; return dummy.next, which is the new head.
Time O(L) Space O(1)

Two passes over the list. Perfectly good, but the follow-up asks for one. In C++ the removed node is deleted; Java and Python free it automatically.

Approach 2: Stack

Push every node (dummy first) onto a stack. The nodes come back off in reverse, so after n pops the top of the stack is the node just before the target.

  • Pushing the dummy means there's always a node left on top, even when the head is removed.
  • It reads the list once, but stores all of it.
Time O(L) Space O(L)

A natural way to "count from the end", but the extra O(L) memory is what the two-pointer trick avoids.

Approach 3: Two Pointers, One Pass Optimal

Keep a fixed gap. If fast is n + 1 nodes ahead of slow, then when fast falls off the end, slow is exactly one node before the n-th from the end.

  • Both start on the dummy. Move fast n + 1 times, then move both until fast is null.
  • Why n + 1, not n: you want to stop before the target so you can change its predecessor's next.
  • Starting from the dummy keeps n = length safe: fast lands exactly on null and slow stays on the dummy.
Time O(L) Space O(1)

One pass and no extra memory: the answer to the follow-up. The same fixed-gap idea finds the middle of a list (fast moves 2, slow moves 1) and the k-th from the end.

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's ListNode is a bare class, so the standard library can't help. Copying the values into an array and rebuilding the list works, but it's slower, uses O(L) memory, and makes new nodes instead of removing one.

Write Approach 3. The dummy node is worth remembering on its own: it removes the "what if it's the head?" case from most linked-list problems.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Count the Length, Then Walk Two passes with a dummy node O(L) O(1) Simple; not one pass
Stack Push all, pop n, top is the predecessor O(L) O(L) One pass, but stores every node
Two Pointers, One Pass Fast starts n + 1 ahead of slow O(L) O(1) Expected answer to the follow-up
21. Merge Two Sorted Lists Easy Linked List Recursion
Key idea: Put a dummy node in front of the answer and keep a tail pointer. While both lists have nodes, attach the smaller head to tail and move on. When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other in one step. Return dummy.next. O(m + n) time, O(1) space.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

You're given the heads of two sorted linked lists, list1 and list2. Merge them into one sorted list made by splicing together the nodes of the two lists, and return its head.

  • Each list has between 0 and 50 nodes.
  • -100 <= Node.val <= 100.
  • Both lists are sorted in non-decreasing order.

Examples: [1,2,4], [1,3,4] → [1,1,2,3,4,4]; [], [] → []; [], [0] → [0].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[], [] [] Both heads are null: return null / None without reading .val.
[], [0] [0] Only list1 is empty: the answer is just list2.
[1], [] [1] The mirror case: list2 is empty. Code that checks only one side breaks here.
[1,2,4], [1,3,4] [1,1,2,3,4,4] Ties at both ends: equal values must both be kept, not merged into one.
[5], [1,2,3] [1,2,3,5] The head of the answer comes from list2, so returning list1 is wrong. A dummy node avoids deciding the head up front.
[1,2,3], [4,5,6] [1,2,3,4,5,6] list1 runs out first, and all of list2 is still left: the leftover must be attached, not dropped.
[-100,0,100], [-100,100] [-100,-100,0,100,100] The extreme values, and negatives: don't start a "smallest so far" at 0.
[2,2,2], [2,2] [2,2,2,2,2] Every value equal: the comparison is always a tie, so <= vs < decides which list goes first, and both must still finish.
50 nodes and 50 nodes 100 nodes The largest input. The recursive version goes about 100 calls deep, which is fine at this size.

Approach 1: Collect, Sort, Relink

Forget that the lists are sorted: put every node in one array, sort the array by value, and link the nodes in that order.

  • It moves the same nodes rather than making new ones, which is what "splicing together the nodes" asks for (and in C++ nothing is leaked).
  • A stable sort keeps list1's node first on a tie. The values come out the same either way.
  • Remember to set the last node's next to null.
Time O((m + n) log(m + n)) Space O(m + n)

Easy to get right, but it throws away the fact that both lists are already sorted. That's exactly what the next two approaches use.

Approach 2: Recursion

The smaller of the two heads must be the first node. What comes after it? The merge of everything that's left, which is the same problem on smaller lists.

  • Base case: if one list is empty, the answer is the other list.
  • Otherwise, if list1.val <= list2.val, set list1.next = merge(list1.next, list2) and return list1; else do the same with list2.
Time O(m + n) Space O(m + n) call stack

Short and clear. Each call handles one node, so the stack grows to m + n frames. Fine for 100 nodes; for very long lists it would overflow the stack (Python's default limit is 1,000 calls).

Approach 3: Iterative with a Dummy Node Optimal

The same choice as the recursion, done in a loop: keep a tail on the last node of the answer and keep attaching the smaller head to it.

  • The dummy node means the first node isn't a special case: the head of the answer is simply dummy.next.
  • When one list runs out, the other is already sorted and every value in it is at least the tail's, so attach all of it at once: tail.next = list1 or list2.
  • Using <= takes list1's node on a tie, which keeps the merge stable.
Time O(m + n) Space O(1)

Each node is looked at once and only pointers change. This merge step is the core of merge sort, and it's reused in Merge k Sorted Lists and Sort List.

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's ListNode is a bare class, so the standard library can't merge it. C++ has std::list::merge and std::merge, and Python has heapq.merge, but they work on std::list, iterators and iterables, not on these nodes. Copying the values out, merging, and building new nodes works, but it makes new nodes instead of splicing the old ones.

Write Approach 3. The dummy node plus tail pointer is the standard way to build any linked list as you go.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Collect, Sort, Relink Array of nodes, stable sort by value O((m + n) log(m + n)) O(m + n) Ignores that the input is sorted
Recursion Smaller head, then merge the rest O(m + n) O(m + n) stack Shortest code; deep on long lists
Iterative with a Dummy Node Tail pointer, attach the smaller head O(m + n) O(1) Expected answer
23. Merge k Sorted Lists Hard Linked List Heap (Priority Queue) Divide and Conquer
Key idea: Never compare against all k heads one by one. Either keep the heads in a min-heap (pop the smallest, push its next node), or merge in pairs like merge sort (k lists → k/2 → k/4 → … → 1) using Merge Two Sorted Lists. Both give O(N log k) for N nodes in total.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

You're given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order. Merge them all into one sorted linked list and return it.

  • 0 <= k <= 10⁴ and each list has 0 to 500 nodes.
  • At most 10⁴ nodes in total (call it N).
  • -10⁴ <= Node.val <= 10⁴, and every list is sorted.

Examples: [[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]] → [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6]; [] → []; [[]] → [].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[] [] No lists at all (k = 0): reading lists[0] is out of range.
[[]] [] One list, and it's empty: lists[0] exists but is null.
[[1,2,3],[],[],[4]] [1,2,3,4] Empty lists in the middle: a heap must skip null heads, or comparing .val crashes.
[[1,4,5],[1,3,4],[2,6]] [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,6] The usual case, with equal values in different lists.
[[5,6],[1,2],[3,4]] [1,2,3,4,5,6] The head of the answer doesn't come from lists[0]. A dummy node avoids picking the head up front.
[[2,2],[2],[2,2,2]] [2,2,2,2,2,2] All ties. In Python 3, a heap of (val, node) tuples compares the nodes on a tie and raises TypeError: add the list index as a tie-breaker.
[[-10000,0,10000],[-10000],[10000]] [-10000,-10000,0,10000,10000] The extreme values: don't start a "smallest so far" at 0 or use a sentinel inside the range.
10⁴ lists of 1 node each 10⁴ nodes The case that sinks merging one list at a time: about 5 × 10⁷ node steps. It took 1.6 s in Python here (3.2 s with all values equal), where the heap took 0.01 s.
One list of 10⁴ nodes + 9,999 empty lists The long list k is huge but almost every list is empty: the answer should cost about N, not k · N.

Approach 1: Collect, Sort, Relink

Ignore that the lists are sorted: put all N nodes in one array, sort it by value, and link the nodes in that order.

  • It reuses the same nodes, so nothing new is allocated (and nothing leaks in C++).
  • Remember to set the last node's next to null.
Time O(N log N) Space O(N)

Simple and fast enough here (N ≤ 10⁴), but it wastes the sorted order and needs an array of every node.

Approach 2: Merge One List at a Time

You already know how to merge two lists (LeetCode 21). Merge the first list into an empty answer, then the second into that, and so on.

  • The catch: every merge walks the whole answer so far again. The nodes from the first list get walked about k times.
  • With k lists of about N / k nodes, that's about N / k · (1 + 2 + … + k) ≈ k · N / 2 steps.
Time O(k · N) Space O(1)

Fine for a few lists. At k = N = 10⁴ it's around 5 × 10⁷ steps: it passed here in C++ and Java (about 0.1 s), but took 1.6 to 3.2 s in Python, which risks Time Limit Exceeded.

Approach 3: Min-Heap of the Heads

The next node of the answer is always the smallest of the k current heads. A min-heap gives that smallest head in O(log k) instead of checking all k.

  • Push the head of every non-empty list.
  • Pop the smallest, attach it to tail, and push its next (if any). The heap never holds more than k nodes.
  • Python's heapq compares whole tuples, so push (val, i, node): the list index i settles ties before Python tries to compare two nodes. C++'s priority_queue puts the largest on top, so its comparator uses >.
Time O(N log k) Space O(k)

The answer most interviewers expect, and the idea behind merging many sorted files on disk (k-way merge). It also works when the lists are streams you can only read from the front.

Approach 4: Divide and Conquer (Merge in Pairs) Optimal

Do what merge sort does: merge the lists in pairs, then merge the results in pairs, until one list is left. Every round halves the number of lists, so there are about log₂ k rounds.

  • In one round each node is in at most one merge, so a round costs O(N). log k rounds give O(N log k).
  • Bottom-up with a step: merge lists[i] with lists[i + step] for i = 0, 2·step, 4·step, …, then double step. The answer ends up in lists[0].
  • No recursion and no heap, so the only extra memory is a few pointers.
Time O(N log k) Space O(1)

As fast as the heap with less memory, and it reuses the two-list merge you already have. It does overwrite entries of the input array, which is fine on LeetCode.

In practice No shortcut

There's no library call that merges LeetCode's ListNode lists. Python's heapq.merge and C++'s std::merge work on iterables and iterators, and would mean copying values out and building new nodes. What the library does give you is the heap: heapq, std::priority_queue and java.util.PriorityQueue.

Write Approach 3 or 4. The heap version is the one to know by heart: "the smallest of k candidates, again and again" is a heap problem.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Collect, Sort, Relink Array of all nodes, sort by value O(N log N) O(N) Ignores that the lists are sorted
Merge One List at a Time mergeTwo into a growing answer O(k · N) O(1) Re-walks the answer every time; slow in Python at k = 10⁴
Min-Heap of the Heads Pop smallest head, push its next O(N log k) O(k) The standard k-way merge
Divide and Conquer Merge in pairs, double the step O(N log k) O(1) Merge sort's idea; no extra structure
25. Reverse Nodes in k-Group Hard Linked List Recursion
Key idea: Keep before, the node just in front of the next group (start it on a dummy). Walk k nodes to find the group's end; if you fall off the list, stop. Otherwise reverse the group with the usual prev/cur flip, starting prev at the node after the group, then set before.next = end and before = first. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the head of a linked list, reverse its nodes k at a time and return the new head. If the number of nodes left at the end is less than k, they stay as they are.

  • The list has n nodes, 1 <= k <= n <= 5000.
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 1000.
  • Change the nodes themselves, not the values inside them.
  • Follow-up: can you do it with O(1) extra memory?

Examples: [1,2,3,4,5], k = 2 → [2,1,4,3,5]; [1,2,3,4,5], k = 3 → [3,2,1,4,5].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1], k = 1 [1] The smallest input: one group of one node.
[1,2,3,4,5], k = 1 [1,2,3,4,5] Groups of one: nothing changes, but the code still has to run every group without breaking links.
[1,2], k = 2 [2,1] The whole list is one group, so the head changes. A dummy node handles that without a special case.
[1,2,3,4,5], k = 3 [3,2,1,4,5] The last 2 nodes are a short group and must not be reversed. Check that k nodes exist before flipping any.
[1,2,3,4,5,6], k = 3 [3,2,1,6,5,4] n is a multiple of k: no leftover, and the last group's old first node must end up pointing to null.
[1,2,3,4,5], k = 2 [2,1,4,3,5] Linking groups together: the first group's new last node (1) must point to the second group's new first node (4), not to 3.
[1,2,3,4,5], k = 5 [5,4,3,2,1] k = n: the whole list is reversed.
[7,7,7,7], k = 2 [7,7,7,7] The values look unchanged, but the nodes must still be reordered. Swapping values instead of nodes isn't allowed.
5,000 nodes, k = 1 Unchanged The most groups: a recursive solution goes 5,001 calls deep, which is over Python's default limit of 1,000.

Approach 1: Array of Nodes

Reversing parts of a linked list is fiddly; reversing parts of an array is easy. Put the nodes in an array, reverse each full block of k in the array, then link the nodes in the array's order.

  • Blocks start at 0, k, 2k, … as long as a whole block fits; a shorter last block is skipped.
  • It moves the nodes (their next pointers), not the values, so it follows the rules.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

Simple and hard to get wrong, but the array costs O(n) extra memory, which the follow-up asks you to avoid.

Approach 2: Recursion

Check that the first k nodes exist. If they do, the rest of the list is the same problem: solve it first, then reverse this group so that its old first node points to the rest's answer.

  • Fewer than k nodes: return head unchanged (this also covers null).
  • Reversing with prev starting at the rest's answer means the group is linked to the rest for free when the flip is done.
  • The group's old last node is its new first: that's what the call returns.
Time O(n) Space O(n / k) call stack

Clear, but one call per group. With Python's default recursion limit (1,000) it raised RecursionError here at n = 5,000 for every k ≤ 5. C++ and Java handled 5,001 calls fine.

Approach 3: In Place with a Dummy Node Optimal

The same steps as the recursion, but front to back in a loop, keeping before, the node just in front of the current group.

  • From before, walk k steps to end. Hitting null means fewer than k nodes are left: return dummy.next.
  • Remember first = before.next and after = end.next. Reverse with prev = after and cur = first until cur reaches after; first ends up pointing to after.
  • Reconnect: before.next = end (the new first), then before = first (the new last) for the next group.
Time O(n) Space O(1)

Each node is visited twice (once to find the group, once to flip it) and only pointers change. This is the answer to the follow-up, and it builds on Reverse Linked List (206) and the dummy node from Remove Nth Node From End of List (19).

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's ListNode is a bare class, so there's no library call to reverse part of it. std::reverse, Collections.reverse and slicing only help once the nodes are in an array, which is Approach 1.

Write Approach 3. The pattern to remember: keep the node before the part you're changing, and start prev at the node after it, so the reversed part is already connected on both sides.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Array of Nodes Reverse blocks in an array, relink O(n) O(n) Simplest; not O(1) memory
Recursion Solve the rest, reverse this group onto it O(n) O(n / k) Too deep for Python's default limit when k is small
In Place with a Dummy Node before / first / end / after, flip, reconnect O(n) O(1) Answer to the follow-up
138. Copy List with Random Pointer Medium Linked List Hash Table
Key idea: The hard part is random: it can point to a node whose copy doesn't exist yet. Either keep a map from each original node to its copy, or put each copy right after its original (A → A′ → B → B′), so the copy of X is always X.next. Then A′.random = A.random.next, and you split the two lists apart at the end.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Each node of a linked list has next and also random, which points to any node in the list or to null. Return a deep copy: new nodes with the same values, where every next and random points to the matching new node.

  • 0 <= n <= 1000
  • -10⁴ <= Node.val <= 10⁴
  • The input is written as [val, random_index] per node, with null for no random pointer

Example: [[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]] → a new list written the same way.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[] [] An empty list: return null.
[[7,null],[13,0],[11,4],[10,2],[1,0]] same shape Copying random straight across (copy.random = node.random) makes the copies point at original nodes: not a deep copy.
[[7,null],[13,0]] same shape In the woven version, random can be null: node.random.next without a check raised AttributeError.
[[1,1],[2,1]] same shape A random pointer can point to the node itself (node 1 here).
[[3,null],[3,0],[3,null]] same shape Values repeat, so they can't identify nodes. Map nodes, not values.
any list, woven version original unchanged Splitting out only the copies leaves the original's next pointers aimed at copies. Put each node.next back during the split.

Approach 1: Map, Two Passes

Pass 1: make a copy of every node and store copies[original] = copy, without linking anything. Pass 2: link each copy, copy.next = copies[node.next] and copy.random = copies[node.random].

  • Making all the copies first means every random target already has a copy when it's linked.
  • Mapping None to None removes the null checks.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the map

The clearest version. At n = 1000 here: Python 0.23 ms, Java 1.2 ms, C++ 0.11 ms.

Approach 2: Map, One Pass

Walk the list once. A helper copy_of(node) returns the node's copy, making it the first time it's asked for. For each node, set next and random of its copy through the helper.

  • A copy may be made early (a random pointing ahead) or reused (pointing behind); the map handles both.
  • Same idea as Clone Graph (133): record the copy as soon as it's made.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the map

One pass, but more map lookups per node, so not faster: at n = 1000, Python 0.4–0.7 ms, Java 4.7–5.6 ms, C++ 0.09 ms.

Approach 3: Weave the Copies In Optimal

Three passes, no map. (1) Insert each copy right after its original: A → A′ → B → B′. (2) For each original X, set X′.random = X.random.next, since the copy of any node is the node right after it. (3) Unweave: point each original back at the next original, and each copy at the next copy.

  • The list itself stands in for the map: "copy of X" is just X.next.
  • Check X.random for null in step 2, and restore the original's next pointers in step 3.
Time O(n) Space O(1) besides the copy

Fastest here, since there's no hashing: at n = 1000, Python 0.2 ms, Java 0.4 ms, C++ 0.02 ms. The usual follow-up after the map version: "can you do it without extra memory?"

In practice Built-ins

Python's copy.deepcopy(head) copies the nodes and keeps random pointing at the right copies, since it keeps its own map from old object to copy. C++ and Java have no deep copy for linked objects.

It copied all 500 test lists correctly here, but it recurses along next: 200 nodes were fine, while 300 raised RecursionError, well under this problem's limit of 1,000. Write Approach 1 or 3.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Map, Two Passes Make all copies, then link through the map O(n) O(n) Clearest
Map, One Pass Make each copy when first needed O(n) O(n) Same idea as Clone Graph
Weave the Copies In A → A′ → B → B′, then split O(n) O(1) extra Expected follow-up; restore the original
141. Linked List Cycle Easy Linked List Two Pointers Hash Table
Key idea: Two pointers: slow moves one node at a time, fast moves two. Without a cycle, fast reaches the end. With one, both end up going around it, fast gains one node per step, and they meet. O(n) time, O(1) memory.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the head of a linked list, return true if some node can be reached again by following next, that is, if the list has a cycle. The tests describe the cycle with pos, the index the tail links back to (-1 = no cycle), but pos is not passed to your function.

  • 0 to 10⁴ nodes; -10⁵ <= Node.val <= 10⁵
  • Follow-up: can you do it with O(1) memory?

Example: [3,2,0,-4], pos = 1 → true (the tail links back to node 1). [1], pos = -1 → false.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[] false head is null. A loop that checks only fast.next crashed here (AttributeError); check fast first.
[1,2], pos = -1 false Even length: fast jumps past the last node to null. Checking only fast.next crashed here too.
[1,2,1], pos = -1 false Values repeat. A set of values said true; store the nodes.
[1], pos = 0 true One node pointing to itself: the smallest cycle.
[1,2], pos = 0 true The whole list is the cycle.
10⁴ nodes, the tail pointing to itself true A long walk to a tiny cycle. Floyd made 29,997 pointer moves here, Brent 16,384.

Approach 1: Remember the Nodes

Walk the list and put each node in a hash set. If a node is already in the set, you've come back to it: a cycle. If you reach null, there is none.

  • Store the node itself (its identity), not its value: different nodes can hold the same value.
  • Easy to write, but the set grows with the list.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

At 10⁴ nodes here: Python 0.5 ms, Java 2.5–2.9 ms, C++ 0.6 ms (the slowest version in C++, because of the hashing). Doesn't meet the O(1)-memory follow-up.

Approach 2: Brent's Method

Keep anchor still and walk runner ahead in rounds of 1, 2, 4, 8, … steps. If runner lands on anchor, it went around a cycle. After each round, anchor jumps to where runner is.

  • Once a round is longer than the cycle, and anchor is inside it, runner comes back to anchor within that round.
  • Only one pointer walks the list, so it makes fewer moves than Floyd: 16,384 vs 29,997 on 10⁴ nodes with a self-loop at the tail, and 10,000 vs 15,000 with no cycle.
Time O(n) Space O(1)

Fewer moves didn't mean faster in Python (0.6–1.3 ms vs Floyd's 0.2–0.4 ms): each step does more bookkeeping. C++ 0.01–0.03 ms, Java 0.5–0.8 ms. Good to know when following next is expensive.

Approach 3: Slow and Fast Pointers (Floyd) Optimal

Move slow one step and fast two steps each round. If fast (or fast.next) is null, the list ends. If they ever point to the same node, there's a cycle.

  • Why they must meet: inside the cycle, the gap between them shrinks by exactly one node per round, so it can't skip past zero.
  • Loop while fast and fast.next: both are needed for the two-step move.
Time O(n) Space O(1)

At 10⁴ nodes: Python 0.2–0.4 ms, Java 0.4–0.5 ms, C++ 0.01–0.02 ms, the fastest here in every language. The expected answer. The same two pointers also find where the cycle starts (Linked List Cycle II).

In practice No shortcut

No standard library function checks a linked list for a cycle. A set (set, unordered_set, HashSet) is the only built-in that helps, as in Approach 1.

Approach 3 is what you'd write: five lines and no extra memory.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Remember the Nodes Hash set of visited nodes O(n) O(n) Store nodes, not values
Brent's Method Runner in rounds of 1, 2, 4, … O(n) O(1) Fewest pointer moves
Slow and Fast Pointers (Floyd) 1 step vs 2 steps until they meet O(n) O(1) Expected answer
143. Reorder List Medium Linked List Two Pointers Stack
Key idea: Three steps you already know: find the middle (slow and fast pointers), reverse the second half, then merge the two halves one node at a time. O(n) time, O(1) memory. Remember to cut the list after the middle, or it loops.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Reorder the list L0 → L1 → … → Ln−1 → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → L2 → Ln−2 → …, in place. You may only change the next links, not the values in the nodes.

  • 1 <= n <= 5 × 10⁴
  • 1 <= Node.val <= 1000

Example: [1,2,3,4] → [1,4,2,3]. [1,2,3,4,5] → [1,5,2,4,3].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1,2,3,4] [1,4,2,3] In the array version, the new last node still points to its old neighbor. Without the final cut, the list looped here: 1 → 4 → 2 → 3 → 4 → …
[1,2,3,4] [1,4,2,3] In the O(1) version, forgetting to cut after the middle made node 3 point to itself after the merge: another endless loop.
[1,2,3,4,5] [1,5,2,4,3] Odd length: the middle node ends up last.
[1] and [1,2] unchanged Nothing to move.
[7,7,7,7] [7,7,7,7] Looks unchanged, but the nodes must be in the new order. Swapping values instead of links isn't allowed.
5 × 10⁴ nodes reordered The largest input. Every approach here is O(n): about 3 ms in Python, under 0.3 ms in C++.

Approach 1: Nodes in an Array

Copy the nodes (not the values) into an array, so the back is easy to reach. Then with i at the front and j at the back, link nodes[i] → nodes[j] → nodes[i + 1], moving both inward until they meet.

  • Finish with nodes[i].next = None: the node that ends up last still points to its old neighbor.
  • The simplest to get right.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

At 5 × 10⁴ nodes here: Python 3.3 ms, Java 3.5 ms, C++ 0.26 ms. Fine in practice; the interviewer will ask for O(1) memory next.

Approach 2: Stack of Nodes

Push every node on a stack; the top is the tail. Walk from the head and, (n − 1) / 2 times, pop the top node and slip it in right after the current node. Then cut the link from the node now on top, which is the new tail.

  • Popping gives the back nodes in exactly the order they're needed.
  • Same memory as Approach 1, a different way to think about it.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

At 5 × 10⁴ nodes: Python 2.6 ms, Java 3.5 ms, C++ 0.31 ms.

Approach 3: Middle, Reverse, Merge Optimal

(1) Find the middle with slow and fast. (2) Cut after it and reverse the second half: 4 → 5 becomes 5 → 4. (3) Merge: take one node from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, until the second half runs out.

  • Stopping when fast.next.next is null puts the extra node of an odd list in the first half, so the second half is never longer.
  • Each step is a classic problem: Middle of the List (876), Reverse Linked List (206), Merge Two Sorted Lists (21).
Time O(n) Space O(1)

At 5 × 10⁴ nodes: Python 2.7 ms, Java 1.8 ms, C++ 0.13 ms, the fastest in C++ and Java. The expected answer.

In practice No shortcut

No standard library reorders a custom linked list. C++'s std::list has reverse and splice, but LeetCode passes its own ListNode, so they don't apply.

Approach 3 is what you'd write in an interview. In everyday code, Approach 1 is shorter and just as fast.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Nodes in an Array Two indexes, front and back O(n) O(n) Cut the last link
Stack of Nodes Pop the tail, insert after the front O(n) O(n) Same memory, another view
Middle, Reverse, Merge Three linked-list classics in a row O(n) O(1) Expected answer; cut after the middle
146. LRU Cache Medium Design Hash Table Linked List
Key idea: A hash map finds a key's entry in O(1); a doubly linked list keeps entries in order of use and moves or removes any of them in O(1). Store nodes in the map, keep the most recent right after a head sentinel, and evict the node just before tail. Each node stores its key so the evicted one can be removed from the map.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Design a cache that holds at most capacity keys. get(key) returns the value, or -1 if it's missing. put(key, value) adds or updates a key; if that makes the cache too big, it removes the least recently used key. Both count as a use. Both must run in O(1) on average.

  • 1 <= capacity <= 3000
  • 0 <= key <= 10⁴, 0 <= value <= 10⁵
  • At most 2 × 10⁵ calls to get and put

Example, capacity 2: put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1) → 1, put(3,3) evicts 2, get(2) → -1, put(4,4) evicts 1, get(1) → -1, get(3) → 3, get(4) → 4.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
The example above 1, -1, -1, 3, 4 A get is a use too. Not moving the key on get evicted 1 instead of 2: said 1, 2, -1, 3, 4.
capacity 2: put(1,1), put(2,2), put(2,20), get(1), get(2) 1, 20 Updating a key that's already there never evicts. Checking "full?" before "already there?" evicted 1: said -1, 20.
capacity 1: put(2,1), get(2), put(3,2), get(2), get(3) 1, -1, 2 Capacity 1: every new key evicts the old one.
get(5) on an empty cache -1 A miss changes nothing.
capacity 3000, 2 × 10⁵ calls - The largest input. Scanning a list on each call took 15.7 s in Python here; the linked-list version took 75 ms.

Approach 1: List in Order of Use

Keep [key, value] pairs in a list, least recently used first. To use a key, find it, remove it and append it at the back. To evict, remove the front.

  • Easy to see that it's right.
  • Finding a key and removing from the middle both scan the list: O(capacity) per call.
Time O(capacity) per call Space O(capacity)

2 × 10⁵ calls with capacity 3000 here: Python 11–16 s, Java 0.4–0.7 s, C++ 0.17–0.22 s. Fails the O(1) requirement.

Approach 2: Timestamps and a Lazy Heap

Each use gets a new time from a counter. A hash map holds each key's value and latest time; a min-heap holds (time, key). To evict, pop from the heap until an entry's time matches its key's current time: older entries are skipped.

  • A key's older entries always have smaller times, so they're popped and skipped before its current one. An evicted key never leaves an entry behind.
  • Old entries are only cleared on eviction. With one key and 199,999 get calls, the heap held 200,000 entries.
Time O(log n) per call (amortized) Space O(number of calls) worst case

n = heap size. Fast in practice: Python 140–180 ms, Java 64–74 ms, C++ 40–43 ms on the 2 × 10⁵-call tests. Not O(1), and its memory isn't bounded by the capacity.

Approach 3: Hash Map + Doubly Linked List Optimal

The map gives a key's node. The list is ordered by use, most recent right after head. get: unlink the node and put it after head. put: update and move an existing node; otherwise, if full, remove tail.prev from the list and the map, then add a new node after head.

  • Doubly linked: removing a node needs its prev, and the map can't give that.
  • Sentinel head and tail nodes mean the list is never empty, so there are no null checks.
  • Check "already there?" before "full?": an update never evicts.
Time O(1) per call Space O(capacity)

Python 73–75 ms, Java 34–39 ms, C++ 25–32 ms on the 2 × 10⁵-call tests. The expected answer, and the classic "design" interview question.

In practice Built-ins

Python's OrderedDict has move_to_end and popitem(last=False). Java's LinkedHashMap with accessOrder = true and removeEldestEntry is an LRU cache already. C++'s std::list is a doubly linked list, and splice moves a node in O(1).

Time O(1) per call Space O(capacity)

Python 50 ms (the fastest Python version here), Java 34 ms, C++ 25–33 ms. What you'd use in real code; in an interview, expect to build Approach 3 yourself. (Python's functools.lru_cache caches a function's results, not a key–value store.)

Comparison

Approach Technique Time per call Space Notes
List in Order of Use Scan, remove, append O(capacity) O(capacity) 15.7 s in Python at full size
Timestamps and a Lazy Heap Skip out-of-date heap entries O(log n) O(calls) worst Heap keeps old entries
Hash Map + Doubly Linked List Map to nodes; move and evict in O(1) O(1) O(capacity) Expected answer
206. Reverse Linked List Easy Linked List Recursion
Key idea: Walk the list once with prev and cur. For each node: save cur.next, point cur.next back at prev, then step both forward. At the end prev is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head.

  • The number of nodes is in [0, 5000]
  • -5000 <= Node.val <= 5000

Example: [1,2,3,4,5] → [5,4,3,2,1]. [1,2] → [2,1]. [] → [].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1,2,3,4,5] [5,4,3,2,1] Setting cur.next = prev before saving cur.next loses the rest of the list: it returned [1].
[1,2,3,4,5] [5,4,3,2,1] The recursive version without head.next = None leaves 1 and 2 pointing at each other: the list read 5,4,3,2,1,2,1,2,… forever.
[] [] head is None: return it as is, don't read head.next.
5000 nodes reversed The recursion goes 5000 calls deep, past Python's default limit of 1000.

Approach 1: Copy the Values, Write Them Back

Walk the list and copy every value into an array. Walk it again and write the values back from the end of the array. The links never change; the values move.

  • Easy to get right, but it's not what "reverse the list" usually means: nodes keep their place.
  • Needs O(n) extra space for the values.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

At 5000 nodes: Python 0.45 ms, C++ 39 µs. Fine here, but an interviewer will ask you to move the links.

Approach 2: Recursion

Reverse everything after head first. Now head.next is the tail of that reversed part, so set head.next.next = head and head.next = None. The last node, found at the bottom, is passed back up as the new head.

  • Short, and a good way to think about lists recursively.
  • One call per node: Python needs sys.setrecursionlimit for 5000 nodes.
Time O(n) Space O(n) call stack

At 5000 nodes: Python 0.61 ms, C++ 64 µs, the slowest here because of the calls. Java handled 5000 deep without trouble.

Approach 3: Three Pointers Optimal

prev holds the reversed part, cur the rest. Each step: nxt = cur.next, cur.next = prev, prev = cur, cur = nxt. When cur is None, prev is the new head.

  • The order matters: save first, flip second, step last.
  • Empty and one-node lists need no special case.
Time O(n) Space O(1)

At 5000 nodes: Python 0.36 ms, C++ 8 µs, the fastest in both. Correct on all 3105 tests in every language.

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's ListNode has no methods. With real lists you'd call list.reverse(), std::reverse or Collections.reverse; C++'s std::forward_list even has reverse(). Here, Approach 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Copy the Values Values out, then back in reverse O(n) O(n) Links never move
Recursion Reverse the rest, hang head at the end O(n) O(n) Don't forget head.next = None
Three Pointers Save, flip, step O(n) O(1) Expected answer
287. Find the Duplicate Number Medium Two Pointers Binary Search Array
Key idea: Read i → nums[i] as a link. Every value is 1..n, so following the links from index 0 never comes back to 0 and must run into a cycle. The repeated value has two links pointing to it, so it's where the cycle begins. Floyd's slow/fast pointers find that entry in O(n) time, O(1) space, without changing nums.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

nums has n + 1 values, each in 1..n. Exactly one value repeats (possibly more than twice). Return it without changing nums and using only O(1) extra space.

  • 1 <= n <= 10⁵

Example: [1,3,4,2,2] → 2. [3,1,3,4,2] → 3. [3,3,3,3,3] → 3.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[2,2,2] 2 The value can repeat more than twice, so some values are missing. "sum(nums) − (1 + … + n)" said 3; wrong on 737 of 3006 tests.
[1,1] 1 The smallest case: n = 1.
[3,1,3,4,2] 3 Sorting would find it, but the problem says not to change nums.

Approach 1: Seen Set

Remember every value; the first one you meet again is the answer. The values are 1..n, so C++ and Java use an array of n flags.

  • Simple and fast, but uses O(n) extra space, which the problem doesn't allow.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

10⁵ values, one repeat: Python 4.0 ms, Java 0.30 ms, C++ 0.06 ms.

Approach 2: Binary Search on the Value

Guess mid and count the values ≤ mid. If there are more than mid, two of them must share a value in 1..mid (pigeonhole), so search left; otherwise search right.

  • O(1) space and nums stays as it is.
  • About 17 counting passes over all 10⁵ values.
Time O(n log n) Space O(1)

10⁵ values: Python 60 ms, Java 1.1 ms, the slowest in both. But C++ took only 0.08 ms, faster than Floyd there: each pass reads the array in order, which the CPU does very quickly.

Approach 3: Floyd's Cycle Detection Optimal

Phase 1: from index 0, move slow one link and fast two links per step until they meet inside the cycle. Phase 2: move slow back to 0 and step both one link at a time. They meet at the cycle's entry, the repeated value.

  • The same trick as Linked List Cycle II, with indexes instead of nodes.
  • Phase 2 works because the distance from 0 to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the entry, plus whole laps.
Time O(n) Space O(1)

10⁵ values, one repeat: Python 3.6 ms, Java 0.79 ms, C++ 0.71 ms. The fastest in Python and Java. In C++ Approach 2 won, probably because these jumps around memory are slow next to reading the array in order.

In practice No shortcut

Without the space rule you'd write Approach 1, or Counter(nums).most_common(1) in Python. With it, Approach 3 is the expected answer.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Seen Set First value met twice O(n) O(n) Breaks the space rule
Binary Search on the Value Count values ≤ mid O(n log n) O(1) Fastest in C++ here
Floyd's Cycle Detection Cycle entry of i → nums[i] O(n) O(1) Expected answer
Stack 5 problems Last in, first out
20. Valid Parentheses Easy String Stack
Key idea: Use a stack of open brackets. Push every opener. For a closer, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener; pop it. At the end the stack must be empty. The most recent open bracket is always the one that has to close next, and that's exactly what a stack's top gives you. O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given a string s of the characters ( ) [ ] { }, return whether it is valid: every open bracket is closed by the same type of bracket, brackets close in the right order, and every closing bracket has an open bracket before it.

  • 1 <= s.length <= 10⁴
  • s contains only ()[]{}.

Examples: "()[]{}" → true; "(]" → false; "([)]" → false; "{[]}" → true.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
")" false A closer with nothing open: check the stack is non-empty before looking at its top, or the code crashes.
"((" false Every character is fine on its own, but brackets are left open: check the stack is empty at the end.
"(]" false The right count, the wrong type.
"([)]" false Each type is balanced on its own, but they cross. Counting each type separately says true; only a stack catches the order.
"){" false Even length, but it starts with a closer.
"(()" false An odd length can never be valid: a quick early exit.
"{[()]}" true Nested three deep: each closer matches the most recent opener.
"()[]{}" true Side by side: the stack empties and refills.
5000 × ( then 5000 × ) true The longest input, nested as deep as it gets. Removing pairs one layer at a time needs 5000 passes.

Approach 1: Remove Matching Pairs Until Nothing Changes

In a valid string there's always a pair like (), [] or {} with nothing between, and removing it leaves a string that's still valid. So keep removing them: valid exactly when nothing is left.

  • Stop when a pass removes nothing, then check whether the string is empty.
  • Removing an inner pair brings its outer brackets together, so the next pass can remove those.
Time O(n²) Space O(n)

Each pass is O(n), and deep nesting needs up to n / 2 passes. It still passes at n = 10⁴: the deepest input took 0.15 s in Python here and about 0.1 s in C++ and Java, against 0.002 s for the stack. Short to write, and a nice way to see why the answer works.

Approach 2: Stack Optimal

Read left to right and keep the brackets that are still open. The one that must close next is always the most recent one, so a stack (last in, first out) is the right shape.

  • Opener: push it.
  • Closer: if the stack is empty, or its top isn't the matching opener, return false. Otherwise pop.
  • At the end, return whether the stack is empty. An odd length can return false straight away.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

One pass. The stack holds at most n / 2 openers on a valid string. The same "most recent unmatched thing" stack shows up in Min Stack (155), Daily Temperatures (739) and expression evaluation.

In practice No shortcut

A standard regular expression can't check nesting to any depth, and no standard library has a bracket checker. The stack is a few lines with list / std::stack / ArrayDeque, which is what you'd write.

In Java, prefer ArrayDeque over the old Stack class, which locks on every call.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Remove Matching Pairs Delete (), [], {} until nothing changes O(n²) O(n) Passes at 10⁴; slow on deep nesting
Stack Push openers, match closers against the top O(n) O(n) Expected answer
84. Largest Rectangle in Histogram Hard Array Stack Monotonic Stack
Key idea: The best rectangle is as tall as its shortest bar, and stretches until a shorter bar on each side. Keep a stack of bars with rising heights. When a shorter bar arrives, pop: the popped bar's right wall is the new bar, its left wall is the bar below it on the stack. A height-0 bar at the end pops everything. O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

heights[i] is the height of bar i in a histogram; every bar is 1 wide. Return the area of the largest rectangle that fits inside the histogram.

  • 1 <= heights.length <= 10⁵ and 0 <= heights[i] <= 10⁴.
  • The largest possible answer, 10⁵ · 10⁴ = 10⁹, fits in a 32-bit int.

Examples: [2,1,5,6,2,3] → 10 (bars 5 and 6, height 5, width 2); [2,4] → 4.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[5] 5 One bar: the rectangle is the bar itself.
[0], [0,0] 0 Height 0 is allowed; the area is 0, not an error.
[1,2,3,4,5] 9 Rising heights: nothing is ever popped during the loop. Without the height-0 bar at the end, the stack is never emptied and the answer comes out 0.
[5,4,3,2,1] 9 Falling heights: every bar pops the one before it right away.
[2,1,2] 3 The best rectangle uses the shortest bar across the whole width. When the stack is empty after a pop, the width is all of 0..i−1; measuring it from the popped bar alone gives 2.
[3,3,3] 9 Equal heights. In Approach 2, at least one pass must pop equal bars (>=). If both passes stop at an equal bar (>), each 3 is boxed in by its neighbours and the answer comes out 3.
[2,1,5,6,2,3] 10 The best rectangle (5 × 2) isn't as tall as the tallest bar (6) or as wide as the whole array (1 × 6 = 6).
10⁵ bars, all 10⁴ 1000000000 The largest answer: 10⁹ still fits in an int, so no long is needed.

Approach 1: Every Pair of Edges

Pick a left edge i, then move the right edge j outward one bar at a time. The rectangle over i..j is as tall as the shortest bar in it, so keep a running minimum instead of recomputing it.

  • Area of i..j = low · (j − i + 1), with low = min(heights[i..j]).
Time O(n²) Space O(1)

Correct, but 5.7 s in Python at only n = 10⁴, and 4.1 s in C++ at n = 10⁵. Too slow for the limits.

Approach 2: Nearest Shorter Bar on Each Side

Turn it around: for each bar, find the widest rectangle that is exactly as tall as it. That rectangle stretches until the nearest shorter bar on the left (left[i]) and on the right (right[i]), so its width is right[i] − left[i] − 1.

  • One pass from the left with a stack: pop every bar that isn't shorter than bar i; what's left on top is left[i].
  • The same pass from the right gives right[i]. Then take the best heights[i] · width.
  • Each index is pushed and popped at most once per pass.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

Easier to get right than Approach 3, since each pass answers one clear question. 44 ms in Python at n = 10⁵.

Approach 3: One Pass with a Monotonic Stack Optimal

Do both sides at once. The stack holds bars with rising heights. When bar i isn't taller than the top, the top bar has found its right wall (i), and its left wall is the bar under it on the stack (shorter, or it would have been popped). Pop it and score height · (i − left − 1).

  • After the last bar, pretend there's one more of height 0 at i = n: it pops everything still waiting.
  • An empty stack after a pop means no shorter bar on the left: left = −1, width i.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the stack

One pass and no extra arrays: 22 ms in Python and 0.8 ms in C++ at n = 10⁵. The same stack, row by row, solves Maximal Rectangle (85).

In practice No shortcut

No library has a "largest rectangle" function, in Python, C++ or Java. Write the stack.

Remember two things: pop while the top isn't shorter, and add the height-0 bar at the end. In Java, ArrayDeque is the stack to use (Stack is old and synchronized).

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Every Pair of Edges Running minimum from each left edge O(n²) O(1) Too slow at n = 10⁵
Nearest Shorter Bar Two stack passes, left[i] and right[i] O(n) O(n) Clearest O(n) answer
One-Pass Stack Pop = right wall found; below it = left wall O(n) O(n) One pass; needs the height-0 bar at the end
150. Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation Medium Array Stack Math
Key idea: One stack. Push every number. On an operator, pop two: the top is the right operand, the one under it the left. Push the result. At the end the stack holds the answer. Division rounds toward zero, so in Python use int(a / b), not a // b.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Evaluate an expression written in Reverse Polish Notation: each operator comes after its two operands, so ["2","1","+","3","*"] means (2 + 1) × 3. Operators are + - * /; division truncates toward zero.

  • 1 <= tokens.length <= 10⁴
  • Numbers are in [-200, 200]; the expression is valid, never divides by zero, and every result fits in 32 bits

Example: ["4","13","5","/","+"] → 6 (4 + 13 / 5). ["10","6","9","3","+","-11","*","/","*","17","+","5","+"] → 22.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
["-7","2","/"] -3 Rounds toward zero. Python's // floors: it said -4. Same for ["7","-2","/"].
["4","13","5","/","+"] 6 The first pop is the right operand. Popping in the wrong order computed 5 / 13 = 0: said 4.
["3","-4","-"] 7 "-4" is a number, not an operator. Testing numbers with isdigit() treated it as "minus" and popped an empty stack.
["5"] 5 No operator at all.
["0","3","/"] 0 Zero divided by something is fine.
9,999 tokens: 1 1 + 1 + … 5000 A recursive solution nests about 5,000 calls deep; Python's limit is 1,000. Without raising it, Python failed already at 1,999 tokens.
9,999 tokens: all numbers, then all + 5000 Rewriting the list from the start each time scans half of it per operator: 651 ms in Python here.

Approach 1: Rewrite the List

Find the first operator. The two items right before it are numbers, its operands. Replace the three items with the result, and repeat until one number is left.

  • Mirrors doing it by hand.
  • Each operator rescans from the start and shifts the rest of the list.
Time O(n²) Space O(n)

On 9,999 tokens with every operator at the end: Python 651 ms, Java 37 ms, C++ 6.4 ms. On the alternating chain the operators are found early, so it's fast (Python 5 ms).

Approach 2: Recursion From the End

The last token is the final operation. Reading backwards, a number is just itself; an operator first evaluates its right operand (the tokens just before it), then its left, then combines them.

  • The expression is a tree, and this walks it from the root.
  • The calls nest as deep as the tree: about n / 2 on a long chain. The Python code raises the recursion limit for that.
Time O(n) Space O(n) call stack

Python 2.4 ms, Java 2–2.4 ms, C++ 0.2 ms on 9,999 tokens. Works, but the deep recursion is a risk the stack version doesn't have.

Approach 3: One Stack Optimal

Go left to right. Push numbers. On an operator, pop b (top) then a, and push a op b. Return the one number left.

  • A number is anything that isn't exactly + - * /: "-4" has length 2.
  • C++ and Java / already truncates toward zero; Python needs int(a / b) (safe here, since values fit in 32 bits).
Time O(n) Space O(n)

Python 1.7–1.9 ms, Java 3–3.5 ms, C++ 0.13–0.15 ms on 9,999 tokens. The expected answer, and the reason RPN exists: it needs no parentheses and no precedence rules.

In practice No shortcut

No standard library evaluates RPN. In Python, a dict from operator to function (operator.add, operator.sub, …) shortens Approach 3, but division still needs a truncating lambda, since operator.floordiv floors.

Approach 3 is what you'd write. Don't build a string for eval: it's slow and unsafe on untrusted input.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Rewrite the List Collapse the first operator, repeat O(n²) O(n) 651 ms in Python at 10⁴ tokens
Recursion From the End Right operand, then left O(n) O(n) stack About n / 2 calls deep
One Stack Push numbers; pop two on an operator O(n) O(n) Expected answer
155. Min Stack Medium Stack Design
Key idea: The minimum only changes when a value is pushed or popped at the top, so remember it per level. Either store (value, minimum at or below) in each entry, or keep a second stack of minimums and push to it when a value is ≤ its top. Everything is O(1).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Design a stack with push(val), pop(), top() and getMin(), which returns the smallest value on the stack. Each must run in O(1).

  • -2³¹ <= val <= 2³¹ - 1
  • pop, top and getMin are only called on a non-empty stack
  • At most 3 × 10⁴ calls

Example: push(-2), push(0), push(-3), getMin() → -3, pop(), top() → 0, getMin() → -2.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
push 0, push 1, push 0, getMin, pop, getMin 0, 0 The minimum is pushed twice. Adding to the min stack only on a strictly smaller value lost it after one pop: IndexError on the second getMin.
push 1000, push 500, pop, getMin 1000 Java: comparing two Integers with == compares objects. It said 500 here, but gave the right answer for small values like 50 and 100, so it passes easy tests. Use .equals.
push 2³¹ − 1, push −2³¹, getMin, pop, getMin -2147483648, 2147483647 The full int range. Tricks that store "value minus minimum" overflow here.
15,000 pushes, then 15,000 getMin - Scanning on each getMin is 2.25 × 10⁸ reads: 4.8 s in Python here.

Approach 1: Scan on getMin

A plain stack. getMin looks at every value and returns the smallest.

  • push, pop and top are O(1); only getMin is slow.
  • Fails the O(1) requirement.
Time getMin O(n), the rest O(1) Space O(n)

15,000 pushes then 15,000 getMin: Python 4.8 s, Java 0.19 s, C++ 12 ms.

Approach 2: Store the Minimum With Each Entry

Push (val, min(val, minimum of the entry below)). The top entry's second number is always the current minimum. Popping reveals an entry that already knows its own minimum.

  • The simplest O(1) design: nothing to keep in sync.
  • Always stores two numbers per value.
Time O(1) per call Space O(n), 2 numbers per entry

Same big run: Python 6 ms, Java 13 ms, C++ 2.3 ms, about 800× faster than Approach 1 in Python.

Approach 3: A Second Stack of Minimums Optimal

Keep all values on stack. On push, also push onto mins if the value is ≤ the top of mins. On pop, if the popped value equals the top of mins, pop that too. getMin is the top of mins.

  • ≤ keeps a copy for every repeat of the minimum, so popping one copy leaves the others.
  • mins is usually small: 13 entries for 15,000 random pushes here. Its worst case is a decreasing sequence, where it holds every value (15,000 of 15,000).
Time O(1) per call Space O(n) worst, usually much less

Same big run: Python 5 ms, Java 10 ms, C++ 2.3 ms. The usual answer, with the ≤ and (in Java) the .equals as the two details to get right.

In practice No shortcut

No standard stack tracks its minimum. A heap gives the minimum, but it can't remove the most recently pushed value, so it doesn't fit.

Approach 2 or 3 is what you'd write. Approach 2 is harder to get wrong; Approach 3 saves memory when minimums change rarely.

Comparison

Approach Technique getMin Space Notes
Scan on getMin Plain stack O(n) O(n) 4.8 s in Python on the big run
Store the Minimum With Each Entry (value, min below) pairs O(1) 2 per entry Simplest O(1)
A Second Stack of Minimums Push to mins when ≤ its top O(1) Usually less Expected answer
739. Daily Temperatures Medium Stack Monotonic Stack Array
Key idea: This is "next greater element". Keep a stack of days still waiting for a warmer day; their temperatures only go down toward the top. Each new day pops every waiting day that's colder (their answer is the gap in days), then waits itself. Every day is pushed and popped once: O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

For each day, return how many days you have to wait for a warmer temperature. If no later day is warmer, the answer for that day is 0.

  • 1 <= temperatures.length <= 10⁵
  • 30 <= temperatures[i] <= 100

Example: [73,74,75,71,69,72,76,73] → [1,1,4,2,1,1,0,0]. [30,40,50,60] → [1,1,1,0].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[40,40] [0,0] The same temperature isn't warmer. Popping with <= instead of < said [1,0]; wrong on 1102 of 3006 tests.
[90,80,70] [0,0,0] Nothing is ever warmer: every day stays on the stack, and stays 0.
[50] [0] One day.
10⁴ falling temperatures all 0 Looking ahead day by day checks every pair: 1.3 s in Python for just 10⁴ days.

Approach 1: Look Ahead From Each Day

For each day i, walk j = i + 1, i + 2, … until temperatures[j] is higher. The answer is j − i, or 0 if you run off the end.

  • Quick when warmer days come soon; quadratic when temperatures keep falling.
Time O(n²) Space O(1) besides the answer

10⁴ falling temperatures: Python 1.3 s, Java 17 ms, C++ 17 ms. At 10⁵ that's 100 times the work: too slow.

Approach 2: Right to Left, Jumping

Fill ans from the right. For day i, start at j = i + 1. If day j isn't warmer, no day before day j's own warmer day can be either, so jump straight to j + ans[j]. If ans[j] is 0, nothing to the right is warmer: stop.

  • No extra structure: ans itself holds the jumps.
  • Each day is jumped over at most once more, so the total is O(n).
Time O(n) Space O(1) besides the answer

10⁵ random days: Python 13.3 ms, Java 0.78 ms, C++ 0.68 ms, slightly ahead of the stack in C++ and Java.

Approach 3: Monotonic Stack Optimal

Go left to right with a stack of day indexes still waiting. While today is warmer than the day on top, pop it and set its answer to i − j. Then push today. Days left at the end keep 0.

  • Store indexes, not temperatures: you need the day to compute the wait.
  • The same pattern solves "next greater element" problems in general.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the stack

10⁵ random days: Python 13.2 ms, Java 0.90 ms, C++ 0.80 ms. About the same as Approach 2, and the one most people know.

In practice No shortcut

No library finds the next greater element. Approach 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Look Ahead From Each Day Scan forward from every day O(n²) O(1) 1.3 s in Python at 10⁴
Right to Left, Jumping Reuse answers as jumps O(n) O(1) No extra memory
Monotonic Stack Pop the colder days O(n) O(n) Expected answer
Trees 15 problems A DFS that returns something to the parent
98. Validate Binary Search Tree Medium Tree DFS Binary Search Tree
Key idea: Checking each node against its own children is not enough: a node must be smaller than every ancestor it sits to the left of, and bigger than every one it sits to the right of. Pass those limits down: going left, the node's value becomes the new upper limit; going right, the new lower limit. Every value must be strictly inside its limits. O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the root of a binary tree, return true if it is a valid binary search tree (BST): for every node, all values in its left subtree are strictly smaller and all values in its right subtree are strictly bigger, and both subtrees are BSTs too.

  • 1 to 10⁴ nodes.
  • -2³¹ <= Node.val <= 2³¹ − 1: the full 32-bit int range.

Examples: [2,1,3] → true; [5,1,4,null,null,3,6] → false (4 is on the right of 5 but smaller than it).

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[5,4,6,null,null,3,7] false Each node is fine next to its own children, but 3 sits on the right of 5 and is smaller. Checking only children says true.
[2,2,2], [1,null,1] false Equal values aren't allowed. Using <= instead of < says true.
[2147483647] true The biggest int is a fine value. Starting the upper limit at INT_MAX rejects it; start past it (a long, or infinity).
[-2147483648] true The smallest int. For the in-order check, starting prev at INT_MIN rejects it: use "no value yet" instead.
[1] true One node is always a BST.
[0,null,-1] false A right child smaller than its parent: the plainest failure.
10⁴ nodes in one line (each the right child of the last) true The tree is 10⁴ deep. Recursion goes 10⁴ calls deep, past Python's default limit of 1000; the iterative in-order walk doesn't recurse.

Approach 1: Check Each Node Against Its Whole Subtrees

Use the definition as it's written: for every node, collect every value in its left subtree and every value in its right subtree, and check they're all smaller or all bigger. Then check the subtrees the same way.

  • Correct, because it's exactly the rule.
  • But each value is collected again for every ancestor above it.
Time O(n²) on a tall tree (O(n log n) on a balanced one) Space O(n)

On a one-line tree it took 0.34 s in Python at 1000 nodes and 2.1 s at 2000; the Python version also copies lists, so it grows even faster. Too slow for 10⁴.

Approach 2: In-Order Walk, Values Must Go Up

An in-order walk (left subtree, node, right subtree) visits a BST's values in sorted order. So walk it and check that each value is bigger than the one before. The first time it isn't, the tree is not a BST.

  • Use a stack instead of recursion: push nodes while going left, pop one, check it, then go to its right child.
  • Keep only the previous value, and start with "none yet" (not INT_MIN, which is a real value here).
Time O(n) Space O(h) for the stack (h = height)

1.1 ms in Python for 10⁴ nodes, even in one line, and it stops at the first value out of order. No recursion, so no depth limit to worry about.

Approach 3: Recursion with Limits Optimal

Pass down the range each node must fit in. The root can be anything. Its left child must be below the root; that child's right child must be below the root and above the child; and so on.

  • check(node, low, high): fail if node.val isn't strictly between them.
  • Recurse left with (low, node.val) and right with (node.val, high).
  • In C++ and Java, use long limits so they can sit past the int range.
Time O(n) Space O(h) call stack

The answer interviewers expect: each node is checked once (1.5 ms for 10⁴ in Python), and the limits say exactly what the rule means. On a 10⁴-deep tree, Python needs sys.setrecursionlimit raised (LeetCode does this for you), or use Approach 2.

In practice No shortcut

No library checks a tree like this. Python, C++ and Java all need the walk written out.

Write Approach 3, and mention Approach 2 when the tree can be very deep. The three traps: check against all ancestors (not just children), use strict <, and keep the limits outside the int range.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Whole Subtrees Collect each subtree's values, compare O(n²) O(n) The definition, done slowly
In-Order Walk Sorted order check with a stack O(n) O(h) No recursion; safe on deep trees
Limits Pass (low, high) down the tree O(n) O(h) The usual answer
100. Same Tree Easy Tree DFS BFS
Key idea: Walk both trees together. At each spot: both missing is a match; only one missing, or different values, is a mismatch; otherwise compare the left children with each other and the right children with each other. O(n), and it stops at the first difference.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, return true if they are the same: the same shape, with the same value at every node.

  • Each tree has 0 to 100 nodes (a tree can be empty).
  • -10⁴ <= Node.val <= 10⁴.

Examples: [1,2,3] and [1,2,3] → true; [1,2] and [1,null,2] → false; [1,2,1] and [1,1,2] → false.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[], [] true Two empty trees are the same. Reading p.val before checking for null crashes here.
[], [0] false Only one is empty. Treating a missing node like a node with value 0 says true.
[1,2], [1,null,2] false The same values, but 2 is on the left in one and on the right in the other. Comparing only the values in order (with no marks for missing children) says true.
[1,2,1], [1,1,2] false The children are swapped: the same set of values, not the same tree.
[12,3], [1,23] false When comparing as text, separate the values: without commas both become "123##…".
[1,1], [1,null,1] false Every value is 1: only the shape differs.
[1], [1] true One node each, with both children missing on both sides.

Approach 1: Write Both Trees as Text, Compare

Turn each tree into a string with a pre-order walk (node, left, right), writing # for every missing child. Two trees are the same exactly when their strings are equal.

  • The # marks are what record the shape; without them [1,2] and [1,null,2] look alike.
  • Put a separator between values, or 12, 3 and 1, 23 blur together.
Time O(n + m) Space O(n + m) for the two strings

Easy to trust, but it always writes out both whole trees, even when the roots already differ. 0.044 ms for two 100-node trees in Python.

Approach 2: Recursion on Both Trees Optimal

Compare the two roots, then ask the same question of the two left children and of the two right children.

  • Both null: true. Exactly one null: false. Different values: false.
  • Otherwise: same(p.left, q.left) and same(p.right, q.right). The and stops at the first false.
Time O(min(n, m)) Space O(h) call stack

Four lines, no extra memory, and it stops at the first difference: 0.019 ms in Python. The same check is the core of Subtree of Another Tree (572).

Approach 3: Queue of Pairs (BFS)

The same checks without recursion: keep a queue of node pairs that should match, starting with (p, q). Take a pair, check it, and add its two child pairs.

  • A pair of two nulls is fine: skip it.
  • In Java, ArrayDeque can't store null, so store each pair as a small array.
Time O(min(n, m)) Space O(width) for the queue

Compares the trees level by level (0.026 ms). Useful when trees can be very deep; here they have at most 100 nodes, so recursion is fine.

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's TreeNode has no equality built in: in Python p == q only checks that they're the same object, in Java equals does the same, and in C++ p == q compares pointers.

Write Approach 2. Check the null cases before reading .val.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Text Pre-order with # for missing children O(n + m) O(n + m) Always writes both trees out
Recursion Compare roots, then left with left, right with right O(min(n, m)) O(h) The usual answer
Queue of Pairs BFS over matching pairs O(min(n, m)) O(width) No recursion
102. Binary Tree Level Order Traversal Medium Tree BFS
Key idea: BFS with a queue, one level at a time. At the start of each round the queue holds exactly one level, so read its size first and pop that many nodes, adding their children to the back. Those children are the next level. O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the root of a binary tree, return its values level by level: a list for the root, then a list for its children, and so on, each list from left to right.

  • 0 to 2000 nodes (the tree can be empty).
  • -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.

Examples: [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] → [[3],[9,20],[15,7]]; [1] → [[1]]; [] → [].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[] [] No levels at all. Putting a null root in the queue without checking gives [[]].
[3,9,20,null,null,15,7] [[3],[9,20],[15,7]] Without reading the queue's size per level, BFS gives one flat list, [3,9,20,15,7].
[1,2,3,4,null,null,5] [[1],[2,3],[4,5]] 4 and 5 have different parents but the same depth: one level holds nodes from different subtrees.
[1,2,null,3,null,4] [[1],[2],[3],[4]] A tree that's one line: every level has one node.
DFS that visits right before left left to right Each level comes out reversed: [[3],[20,9],[7,15]].
2000 nodes in one line 2000 levels 2000 deep: recursive DFS passes Python's default limit of 1000. BFS has no depth limit.

Approach 1: DFS with the Depth

Walk the tree in pre-order (node, left, right), passing the depth. Put each value into result[depth]. Because left is always visited before right, every level fills up from left to right.

  • When depth == len(result), this is the first node at that depth: add a new empty list.
Time O(n) Space O(h) call stack

Short, and correct even though it never visits a level all at once. On a 2000-deep line it hit Python's recursion limit (LeetCode raises it, so it passes there).

Approach 2: BFS with a Queue Optimal

A queue serves nodes in the order they arrive, so it visits the tree level by level. To know where one level ends, count: at the start of each round, len(queue) is exactly the number of nodes on this level.

  • Pop that many nodes, saving their values, and add their children to the back.
  • After the round, only the next level is left in the queue.
