Time O(n) Space O(w), the widest level

The standard answer: 0.18 ms for 2000 nodes in Python, and no recursion. The same loop solves Right Side View (199), Zigzag (103) and Average of Levels (637).

Approach 3: Two Lists, This Level and the Next

Skip the counting: keep the current level as a plain list. Its values are one answer list; its children, in order, make the next level. Repeat until a level is empty.

  • No queue needed, and no level size to remember.
Time O(n) Space O(w)

The same speed as Approach 2 (0.15 ms) and maybe easier to read: each loop is exactly one level.

In practice No shortcut

No library walks a tree by levels, but each has a good queue: collections.deque in Python (list.pop(0) is O(n)), std::queue in C++, ArrayDeque in Java.

Write Approach 2. Return [] for an empty tree, and read the queue's size before the inner loop, not inside it (it changes as children are added).

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
DFS with Depth Pre-order, result[depth].append O(n) O(h) Short; recursion depth limit
BFS Queue Pop len(queue) nodes per round O(n) O(w) The usual answer
Two Lists This level → its children O(n) O(w) No queue, no counting
104. Maximum Depth of Binary Tree Easy Tree DFS BFS
Key idea: A tree's depth is 1 (this node) + the deeper of its two subtrees, and an empty tree has depth 0. That's three lines of recursion, O(n). On a very deep tree, count the levels with BFS instead, so there's no recursion at all.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth: the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf.

  • 0 to 10⁴ nodes (the tree can be empty).
  • -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

Examples: [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] → 3; [1,null,2] → 2.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[] 0 No nodes. Reading root.left without checking crashes.
[0] 1 One node is depth 1: the answer counts nodes, not edges.
[3,9,20,null,null,15,7] 3 Counting edges (a leaf as 0) gives 2.
[1,null,2] 2 The left side is empty. Taking the min of the two sides by mistake gives 1.
[1,2,3,null,null,null,4,null,5] 4 The deepest path isn't on the left: both sides must be checked.
10⁴ nodes in one line 10000 10⁴ deep: plain recursion passes Python's default limit of 1000. BFS or a stack has no such limit.

Approach 1: BFS, Count the Levels

The depth is the number of levels. Walk the tree level by level with a queue, as in Level Order Traversal (102), and add 1 for each level.

  • At the start of each round the queue holds exactly one level: pop that many nodes, adding their children.
Time O(n) Space O(w), the widest level

No recursion, so a 10⁴-deep line is no problem (1.4 ms in Python).

Approach 2: Recursion Optimal

Ask each subtree for its depth and add 1 for the current node: 1 + max(depth(left), depth(right)). An empty subtree answers 0, which makes a leaf come out as 1.

  • Every node is visited once, after both its children (post-order).
Time O(n) Space O(h) call stack

The answer interviewers expect, and the base of many tree problems: Balanced Binary Tree (110) and Diameter of Binary Tree (543) use the same height. On a 10⁴-deep line it hit Python's recursion limit (LeetCode raises the limit, so it passes there).

Approach 3: DFS with a Stack

The same depth-first walk without recursion: push (node, depth) pairs on a stack, and keep the biggest depth seen.

  • Push the right child first, so the left one is popped first (the same order as the recursion).
Time O(n) Space O(h) for the stack

Depth first like Approach 2, but safe on deep trees (1.3 ms for the 10⁴-deep line).

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's TreeNode has no height or depth built in, in any of the three languages.

Write Approach 2. Return 0 for an empty tree, and use max, not min (that's 111, Minimum Depth, and it needs extra care for nodes with one child).

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
BFS Levels Count rounds of a level-by-level queue O(n) O(w) No recursion
Recursion 1 + max(left, right) O(n) O(h) The usual answer
DFS Stack (node, depth) pairs, keep the max O(n) O(h) Depth first, no recursion
105. Construct Binary Tree from Preorder and Inorder Traversal Medium Tree Hash Table Divide and Conquer
Key idea: preorder[0] is the root. Find it in inorder: everything to its left there is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree. Repeat on each part. A map from value to inorder index makes each lookup O(1), and taking the roots from preorder one by one (left subtree first) avoids copying: O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the preorder (node, left, right) and inorder (left, node, right) lists of the same binary tree, build the tree and return its root.

  • 1 to 3000 nodes; -3000 <= value <= 3000.
  • All values are different (that's what makes the tree unique).
  • Both lists really come from the same tree.

Example: preorder = [3,9,20,15,7], inorder = [9,3,15,20,7] → [3,9,20,null,null,15,7].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input (preorder, inorder) Expected Why it's tricky
[-1], [-1] [-1] One node: both subtrees are empty parts.
[1,2], [2,1] [1,2] The root is last in inorder: the right part is empty.
[1,2], [1,2] [1,null,2] The same preorder, but now the root is first in inorder: 2 goes on the right. Only inorder tells left from right.
The example, building the right subtree first [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] Preorder lists the whole left subtree before the right. Taking roots from it in the wrong order uses the wrong values, and here it runs off the end of preorder (IndexError).
The example, slicing preorder as [1:k] same as above The left subtree has k values, so its part of preorder is [1:k+1]. One short, and a value goes looking for itself in the wrong part of inorder (ValueError).
3000 nodes in one line 3000 deep The recursion goes 3000 deep, past Python's default limit of 1000 (LeetCode raises it). Slicing also copies ~n values per level: 63 ms here against 2 ms.

Approach 1: Recursion with Slices

Take the root from preorder[0] and find its index k in inorder. The left subtree has exactly k values: the next k in preorder (preorder[1:k+1]) and the first k in inorder. The rest is the right subtree. Build both the same way.

  • An empty list means an empty subtree: return None.
Time O(n²) worst (searching and copying at every level) Space O(n²) worst for the copies

The clearest way to see the idea. On a balanced tree it's fine (2 ms for 3000 random nodes), but on a 3000-node line it took 63 ms.

Approach 2: Index Map and Bounds Optimal

Remove both costs. A map value → inorder index replaces the search. Instead of slicing, pass the bounds lo..hi of the inorder part. And the roots don't need slicing either: preorder gives them in exactly the order the recursion asks for them, so keep one counter into it.

  • build(lo, hi): take the next preorder value as the root, find k, then build(lo, k − 1) and build(k + 1, hi).
  • Build the left subtree first, or the counter hands out the wrong roots.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the map, O(h) stack

The answer interviewers expect: 1.1 ms for 3000 random nodes and 2.1 ms for the long line. The same idea works for Construct from Inorder and Postorder (106), where postorder gives the roots from the end.

Approach 3: One Pass with a Stack

Walk preorder once with a stack of nodes that may still get a right child, and a pointer j into inorder. Each new value is the left child of the top, unless the top's value is inorder[j]: then the top's left side is finished, so pop while the top matches inorder (moving j), and the new value is the right child of the last node popped.

  • Inorder reaching a node's value means everything to its left is already built.
  • No recursion and no map.
Time O(n): each node is pushed and popped once Space O(h) for the stack

The fastest here (0.6–0.9 ms) and safe on deep trees, but harder to explain than Approach 2.

In practice No shortcut

No library builds a tree from its traversals, in Python, C++ or Java. Use a hash map for the inorder positions: a dict, unordered_map or HashMap.

Write Approach 2. The two traps: build left before right, and give the left part exactly k values. It only works because the values are all different: with repeats, the root's position in inorder is ambiguous.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Slices Find the root in inorder, slice both lists O(n²) O(n²) Clearest; slow on deep trees
Map and Bounds value → index map, preorder counter O(n) O(n) The usual answer
Stack Left child unless inorder says climb O(n) O(h) No recursion, no map
110. Balanced Binary Tree Easy Tree DFS
Key idea: A tree is balanced when at every node the two subtree heights differ by at most 1. Compute the heights bottom-up in one walk, and return -1 as soon as a node fails, so the answer travels up without more work. O(n), instead of recomputing heights for every node.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given a binary tree, return true if it is height-balanced: for every node, the heights of its left and right subtrees differ by no more than 1.

  • 0 to 5000 nodes (the tree can be empty).
  • -10⁴ <= Node.val <= 10⁴.

Examples: [3,9,20,null,null,15,7] → true; [1,2,2,3,3,null,null,4,4] → false; [] → true.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[] true An empty tree has nothing out of balance.
[1,2] true Heights 1 and 0: a difference of 1 is allowed.
[1,2,null,3] false At the root, the sides are 2 and 0. It has only one leaf, so the rule "all leaves within one level of each other" wrongly says true.
[1,2,2,3,null,null,3,4,null,null,4] false The root's two sides are both height 3, so checking only the root says true. The 2's below it are unbalanced: every node must pass.
[1,2,2,3,3,null,null,4,4] false The left side is height 3, the right 1: the problem is at the root.
5000 nodes in one line false It fails near the bottom, but the recursion has to go 5000 deep to get there, past Python's default limit of 1000. The stack version is fine.

Approach 1: Check Every Node from the Top

Follow the definition: at the root, compute the height of each side and compare them. Then check the left and right subtrees the same way.

  • height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)), with an empty tree at 0.
  • The root passing is not enough: recurse into both children too.
Time O(n · h): each height is recomputed for every node above it Space O(h) call stack

Correct, and close to the definition, but it repeats work: 9.6 ms for a balanced tree of 5000 nodes, 12 times slower than Approach 2.

Approach 2: Bottom-Up with −1 for "Not Balanced" Optimal

Compute each subtree's height once, children first, and check the node at the same moment. One function can return both answers: the height if the subtree is balanced, or -1 if it isn't.

  • If either child returns -1, return -1 right away: there's no need to look further.
  • Otherwise compare the two heights, then return 1 + max(left, right).
Time O(n) Space O(h) call stack

The answer interviewers expect: each node is visited once (0.8 ms for 5000 balanced nodes). It's Maximum Depth (104) with one check added.

Approach 3: Post-Order with a Stack

The same bottom-up check without recursion. Each node goes on the stack twice: the first time, push it back marked "children done", then its children; the second time, both children's heights are already stored, so check and store its own.

  • Keep the heights in a map from node to height; a missing child counts as 0.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the map

A little slower than Approach 2 (1.4 ms), but safe on a 5000-deep tree (0.7 ms), where both recursive versions passed Python's limit.

In practice No shortcut

Nothing in Python, C++ or Java checks a tree's balance. Self-balancing trees (like std::map or Java's TreeMap, both red-black trees) keep themselves balanced, but use a looser rule than this one.

Write Approach 2. Check every node, not just the root, and allow a difference of exactly 1.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Top-Down Compare heights at each node, recompute each time O(n · h) O(h) Follows the definition; repeats work
Bottom-Up, −1 Height or −1, children first O(n) O(h) The usual answer
Stack Post-order, heights in a map O(n) O(n) No recursion
124. Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum Hard Tree DFS Dynamic Programming
Key idea: Every path has one highest node, where it bends. For each node, ask each child for its best path going down one side, dropping a side that's negative (max(0, …)). The path bending here is val + left + right: compare it with the best so far. Return only val + max(left, right) to the parent, since a path can't fork. O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

A path is a chain of nodes, each joined to the next by an edge, with no node used twice. It doesn't have to go through the root. Return the biggest sum of values along any non-empty path.

  • 1 to 3 × 10⁴ nodes; -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000.
  • A path can be a single node.

Examples: [1,2,3] → 6 (2 → 1 → 3); [-10,9,20,null,null,15,7] → 42 (15 → 20 → 7).

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[-3] -3 The path can't be empty. Starting the best at 0 says 0; start it at the root's value.
[-1,-2,-3] -1 Every value is negative: the answer is the single biggest node.
[1,-2,3] 4 Skip the −2 side: 1 → 3. Keeping negative sides (no max(0, …)) says 3.
[1,2,3,4,5] 11 4 → 2 → 5 bends at 2, then can't also go up to 1. Returning both sides to the parent says 15, a "path" that forks.
[-10,9,20,null,null,15,7] 42 The best path doesn't touch the root.
[10,9,-100,null,null,1,1] 19 9 → 10, leaving out a whole side whose best is −99.

Approach 1: Try Every Node as the Bend

For each node, imagine the path bends there. Its best value is the node plus the best way down on the left plus the best way down on the right (each at least 0). down(node) works out a way down from scratch.

  • down(node) = val + max(0, down(left), down(right)): a way down may stop at node.
  • Visit every node and keep the biggest.
Time O(n · h): every node's subtrees are measured again Space O(h)

94 ms on 3 × 10⁴ random nodes, but on a long line it's O(n²): 1.3 s at 4000 nodes, so roughly a minute at 3 × 10⁴.

Approach 2: One Walk, Best Gain Up Optimal

Do it all in one post-order walk. gain(node) returns the best path starting at node and going down one side. On the way, the node checks the path that bends at it, using both children's gains.

  • left = max(0, gain(left)), the same for right.
  • Update best with val + left + right.
  • Return val + max(left, right): the parent can extend only one side.
Time O(n) Space O(h) call stack

The answer interviewers expect (10 ms for 3 × 10⁴ nodes). The same "check here, return one side up" shape as Diameter of Binary Tree (543).

Approach 3: Post-Order with a Stack

The same work without recursion: each node goes on the stack twice. The second time, both children's gains are already stored, so check the bend and store its own gain.

  • A missing child has gain 0.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the gains

16 ms for 3 × 10⁴ nodes. A tree that's one long line of 3 × 10⁴ nodes is 3 × 10⁴ deep, past Python's default recursion limit; this version doesn't care.

In practice No shortcut

No library finds paths in a tree like this, in Python, C++ or Java.

Write Approach 2. The three traps: start best at the root's value (not 0), drop negative sides, and send only one side up.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Every Bend Each node as the top, recompute the ways down O(n · h) O(h) O(n²) on a long line
One Walk Check the bend, return one side up O(n) O(h) The usual answer
Stack Post-order, gains in a map O(n) O(n) No recursion
199. Binary Tree Right Side View Medium Tree Breadth-First Search Depth-First Search
Key idea: From the right you see the last node of each level, and it isn't always a right child: a left child shows when nothing is to its right. Either take the last node of each BFS level, or DFS right child first and keep the first node reached at each new depth.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Standing on the right side of a binary tree, return the values you can see from top to bottom.

  • The number of nodes is in [0, 100]
  • -100 <= Node.val <= 100

Example: [1,2,3,null,5,null,4] → [1,3,4]. [1,2,3,4,null,null,null,5] → [1,3,4,5]. [] → [].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1,2,3,4] [1,3,4] 4 is a left child but nothing is to its right. Walking only .right from the root said [1,3]; it was wrong on 2496 of 3307 tests.
[82,70,92] [82,92] The DFS visiting left before right gives the left side view: it said [82,70].
[] [] An empty tree: don't put None in the queue.
100 nodes, all left children all 100 values Every node is the only one on its level, so all of them show.

Approach 1: Store Every Level

Build the levels one after another: the next level is the children of this one, left to right. Keep all the values, then take the last one from each level.

  • Simple and correct, but it stores every value just to use one per level.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

Average over 3307 trees (up to 100 nodes): Python 3.0 µs, C++ 2.1 µs, Java 1.0 µs. The slowest in each language: it builds a new list per level.

Approach 2: BFS, Last of Each Level

Use a queue. At the start of each round it holds exactly one level, so note its size and pop that many nodes, pushing their children. The node popped at k == size − 1 is the rightmost.

  • Saving size first matters: the queue grows while you pop.
Time O(n) Space O(width)

Average: Python 2.0 µs, C++ 0.47 µs, Java 0.63 µs.

Approach 3: DFS, Right Child First Optimal

Walk the tree depth first, visiting the right child before the left, and carry the depth. The first node reached at a new depth (depth == len(res)) is the rightmost one there, because everything to its right was visited earlier.

  • len(res) is the number of depths seen so far, so no set is needed.
  • The calls go as deep as the tree: 100 at most here.
Time O(n) Space O(height)

Average: Python 2.6 µs, C++ 0.30 µs, Java 0.32 µs, the fastest in C++ and Java. In Python, function calls make it a bit slower than Approach 2.

In practice No shortcut

There's no built-in tree type to ask. Approach 2 or 3 is what you'd write; both are about ten lines.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Store Every Level All levels, then the last of each O(n) O(n) Stores more than it needs
BFS, Last of Each Level Pop size nodes, keep the last O(n) O(width) Fastest in Python
DFS, Right Child First First node at each new depth O(n) O(height) Shortest code
226. Invert Binary Tree Easy Tree Depth-First Search Breadth-First Search
Key idea: Mirroring a tree means swapping the left and right child of every node. Visit each node once (by recursion or a queue) and swap its two children. O(n) time. With recursion, read both subtrees before changing either one.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Invert a binary tree (mirror it left to right) and return its root.

  • The number of nodes is in [0, 100]
  • -100 <= Node.val <= 100

Example: [4,2,7,1,3,6,9] → [4,7,2,9,6,3,1]. [2,1,3] → [2,3,1]. [] → [].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1,2] [1,null,2] root.left = invert(root.right) then root.right = invert(root.left) reads the left side after it was overwritten: it said [1]. Wrong on 2846 of 3205 tests.
[4,2,7,1,3,6,9] [4,7,2,9,6,3,1] The same bug gives [4,7,7,9,9,9,9]: both children end up as the same node.
[73,22,null,2] [73,null,22,null,2] Swapping only the root's children isn't enough: 22's children must swap too.
[] [] An empty tree: return None, don't touch root.left.

Approach 1: Build a Mirrored Copy

mirror(node) makes a new node with the same value. Its left child is mirror(node.right) and its right child is mirror(node.left). The input tree stays as it was.

  • Useful when the caller still needs the original.
  • Uses a second tree's worth of memory.
Time O(n) Space O(n) for the new tree

Average over 3206 trees: Python 2.6 µs, C++ 0.30 µs, Java 0.18 µs. The slowest in Python and C++, because of the new nodes.

Approach 2: BFS With a Queue

Put the root in a queue. Pop a node, swap its children, and queue them. When the queue is empty, every node has been swapped.

  • No recursion, so a very deep tree can't overflow the stack.
  • The order doesn't matter: any visit order that reaches every node works.
Time O(n) Space O(width) for the queue

Average: Python 1.9 µs, C++ 0.23 µs, Java 0.43 µs.

Approach 3: Recursive Swap Optimal

Invert both subtrees and put each on the other side, in place. In Python, one tuple assignment reads both calls before assigning either side; Java keeps them in variables; C++ swaps the children first and then inverts each one.

  • The shortest code. With at most 100 nodes, the recursion depth is never a problem here.
Time O(n) Space O(height) call stack

Average: Python 1.6 µs, C++ 0.12 µs, Java 0.14 µs, the fastest in every language.

In practice No shortcut

No standard library has a binary tree to mirror. Approach 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Build a Mirrored Copy New tree, sides crossed O(n) O(n) Leaves the input unchanged
BFS With a Queue Pop, swap, queue the children O(n) O(width) No recursion
Recursive Swap Invert both sides, then cross them O(n) O(height) Expected answer
230. Kth Smallest Element in a BST Medium Binary Search Tree Depth-First Search Stack
Key idea: An in-order walk of a BST (left subtree, node, right subtree) visits the values in sorted order. Walk it with a stack and stop at the k-th node you pop: O(h + k) time, O(h) space, where h is the tree's height.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the root of a binary search tree and k, return the k-th smallest value in it (counting from 1).

  • 1 <= k <= n <= 10⁴
  • 0 <= Node.val <= 10⁴

Example: [3,1,4,null,2], k = 1 → 1. [5,3,6,2,4,null,null,1], k = 3 → 3.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[2,1], k = 2 2 Pre-order (node first) isn't sorted: it said 1. Reading the level-order list as if it were sorted fails the same way; wrong on 2400 of 3105 tests.
10⁴ nodes, each the left child of the last - The tree is one long chain. The recursive Python versions hit RecursionError at the default limit of 1000, so they raise it.
[1], k = 1 1 One node.
10⁴ nodes, k = n the largest No early stop helps: every node is visited.

Approach 1: List Every Value In Order

Do a full in-order walk, appending each value. The list comes out sorted, so the answer is vals[k − 1].

  • Simple, but it visits all n nodes even when k is 1.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

10⁴ random values, k = 1: Python 1.2 ms, Java 0.13 ms, C++ 0.08 ms; about the same for any k.

Approach 2: Recursive In-Order, Stop Early

Same walk, but count down from k as each value is visited. At 0, save the value and make every remaining call return straight away.

  • No list of values; the work is about h + k nodes.
  • The early-stop flag must be checked after the left call, or the walk keeps going.
Time O(h + k) Space O(h) call stack

10⁴ random values, k = 1: Python 2.4 µs, Java 0.5 µs, C++ 0.1 µs, 500 times faster than Approach 1 in Python. With k = n it's no faster.

Approach 3: Iterative In-Order With a Stack Optimal

Push nodes while going left. Pop: that's the next smallest value. If it's the k-th pop, return it; otherwise move to its right child and repeat.

  • No recursion, so a 10⁴-node chain is fine in every language.
  • The stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path.
Time O(h + k) Space O(h)

10⁴ random values, k = n: Python 1.0 ms (the fastest in Python), Java 0.10 ms, C++ 0.06 ms (about the same as Approach 2). A 10⁴ chain with k = 1: Python 0.36 ms, against 1.7 ms for Approach 2.

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's TreeNode has no methods. A sorted structure like Java's TreeSet or C++'s std::set doesn't give the k-th element directly either.

Follow-up (many inserts and queries): store each node's subtree size, then pick the side by comparing k with the left size, O(h) per query.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
List Every Value Full in-order, then index O(n) O(n) Same cost for any k
Recursive, Stop Early Count down to 0 O(h + k) O(h) Needs a higher recursion limit in Python
Iterative With a Stack Push left, pop, go right O(h + k) O(h) Expected answer
235. Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree Medium Binary Search Tree Tree
Key idea: In a BST, values tell you which way a node is. Walk down from the root: if p and q are both smaller, go left; if both bigger, go right. The first node where they're not on the same side (or that is one of them) is the answer. O(h) time, O(1) space.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given a BST and two of its nodes p and q, return their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both below it. A node counts as its own ancestor.

  • 2 <= n <= 10⁵; all values are different
  • p != q, and both are in the tree

Example: [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5], p = 2, q = 8 → 6. Same tree, p = 2, q = 4 → 2. [2,1], p = 2, q = 1 → 2.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[2,1], p = 2, q = 1 2 p is the ancestor of q. Stopping only when p < node < q (strictly) walked past it and returned nothing; wrong on 1915 of 3003 tests.
p = 2, q = 4 in the example tree 2 The same: the answer is p itself.
10⁵ nodes in one chain, the two deepest the second deepest h = n: walking down takes 10⁵ steps. A recursive walk would also go 10⁵ calls deep.

Approach 1: Parent Pointers (Any Binary Tree)

Walk the whole tree and record each node's parent. Put p and all its ancestors in a set. Climb from q until you reach a node in that set.

  • Doesn't use the BST order, so it works on any binary tree.
  • Visits all n nodes even when the answer is the root.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

10⁵ random values: Python 18 ms, Java 20 ms, C++ 7.3 ms, about 700 times slower than Approach 3 in Python.

Approach 2: Compare the Two Search Paths

Search for p from the root (smaller left, bigger right) and keep the path. Do the same for q. Both paths start the same way; the last node they share is the answer.

  • Uses the BST order: only two root-to-node paths are walked.
  • Keeps both paths, O(h) memory.
Time O(h) Space O(h)

A 10⁵-node chain: Python 13.5 ms, Java 3.0 ms, C++ 1.2 ms. On the random tree (h about 40): Python 26 µs.

Approach 3: Walk Down to the Split Point Optimal

Start at the root. If both values are smaller than the node, go left; if both are bigger, go right. Otherwise this node is between them, or is one of them: return it.

  • One walk, no lists, no recursion.
  • Everything below the split point is on one side of it, so nothing deeper can hold both.
Time O(h) Space O(1)

A 10⁵-node chain: Python 5.5 ms, Java 0.23 ms, C++ 0.13 ms, the fastest in every language.

In practice No shortcut

No library works on LeetCode's TreeNode. Approach 3 is a few lines and is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Parent Pointers Ancestors of p, climb from q O(n) O(n) Works on any binary tree
Compare the Search Paths Last node both paths share O(h) O(h) Uses the BST order
Walk Down to the Split Both smaller: left; both bigger: right O(h) O(1) Expected answer
297. Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree Hard Tree Design Depth-First Search
Key idea: Write the values in pre-order (node, left subtree, right subtree) and mark every empty spot with "#". The markers tell exactly where each subtree ends, so reading the tokens back in the same order rebuilds the same tree. O(n) both ways. Use a stack instead of recursion so a 10⁴-deep tree is fine.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Build a Codec whose serialize(root) turns a binary tree into a string, and whose deserialize(data) turns that string back into the same tree. Any format works, as long as the round trip is exact.

  • The number of nodes is in [0, 10⁴]
  • -1000 <= Node.val <= 1000

Example: [1,2,3,null,null,4,5] → (any string) → the same tree. [] → the empty tree.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1,2] and [1,null,2] two different strings Writing only the values, level by level, gives 1,2 for both: you can't tell left from right. Empty spots must be written too.
10⁴ nodes in one chain - The recursive version hit RecursionError in Python at the default limit of 1000, so it raises the limit. The stack version needs nothing.
[] [] An empty tree must survive the round trip too.
[-1000,1000] the same Negative values: separate tokens with commas instead of relying on fixed widths.

Approach 1: Level Order With "null"

Write the tree level by level, with "null" for each missing child, and drop trailing nulls (this is LeetCode's own format). To rebuild, keep a queue of parents: each parent takes the next two tokens as its left and right child.

  • The string is easy to read and matches how LeetCode shows trees.
  • No recursion either way.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

10⁴ random nodes, round trip: Python 7.2 ms, Java 3.0 ms, C++ 1.6 ms. 93,856 characters: "null" is longer than "#".

Approach 2: Recursive Pre-order With "#"

walk(node) writes "#" for None, or the value followed by walk(left) and walk(right). To rebuild, build() reads one token: "#" means None; otherwise make the node, then build() its left and its right.

  • The two functions mirror each other, which makes it easy to get right.
  • One call per node and per "#": Python needs a higher recursion limit for deep trees.
Time O(n) Space O(height) call stack

10⁴ random nodes, round trip: Python 6.2 ms, Java 1.9 ms, C++ 1.3 ms, the fastest in Python and Java. 63,863 characters, a third shorter than Approach 1.

Approach 3: Pre-order With a Stack Optimal

The same string as Approach 2, made with a stack (push right, then left). To rebuild, keep a stack of nodes still missing a child, with a count of children given. Each token becomes the top node's next child; a node with both children set is popped, and a real new node is pushed.

  • No recursion, so a 10⁴-node chain needs no special setup in any language.
  • The stack holds at most one root-to-leaf path.
Time O(n) Space O(height)

10⁴ random nodes, round trip: Python 9.2 ms, Java 2.9 ms, C++ 1.3 ms (the fastest in C++). A little slower than Approach 2 in Python and Java, in exchange for not depending on the recursion limit.

In practice No shortcut

Outside LeetCode you'd usually pick an existing format such as JSON. Here you write the format yourself; Approach 2 or 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Level Order With "null" BFS; parents take the next two tokens O(n) O(n) LeetCode's own format
Recursive Pre-order walk / build mirror each other O(n) O(height) Needs a higher limit in Python
Pre-order With a Stack Same string, no recursion O(n) O(height) Safe for any depth
543. Diameter of Binary Tree Easy Tree DFS
Key idea: Every path has one highest node where it bends: it goes down the left side and down the right side. So the longest path bending at a node has height(left) + height(right) edges. One post-order DFS returns each node's height to its parent and, on the way, keeps the largest left + right it sees. O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the root of a binary tree, return the length of its diameter: the longest path between any two nodes. The length is the number of edges on the path, and the path may or may not pass through the root.

  • The tree has between 1 and 10⁴ nodes.
  • -100 <= Node.val <= 100.

Examples: [1,2,3,4,5] → 3 (4 – 2 – 1 – 3 or 5 – 2 – 1 – 3); [1,2] → 1.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1] 0 One node, no edges. Counting nodes instead of edges gives 1.
[1,2] 1 The path ends at the root: one side has height 0.
[1,2,3,4,5] 3 The usual case: the path bends at the root.
[1,2,null,3,4,5,null,null,6] 4 The longest path (5 – 3 – 2 – 4 – 6) bends at 2 and skips the root. Only checking the root gives 3.
[1,2,null,3,null,4,null,5] 4 A chain: the path runs from the root straight down to the leaf.
[1,2,3,4,5,6,7] 4 A full tree: leaf to leaf through the root, 2 + 2 edges.
[-1,-2,-3] 2 The values don't matter, only the shape. Don't add up vals.
A chain of 10⁴ nodes 9999 The deepest tree: recursion goes 10⁴ calls deep (over Python's default limit of 1,000), and recomputing heights at every node gets slow.

Approach 1: Brute Force (Heights from Scratch at Every Node)

Try every node as the bend. For each one, compute the heights of its two subtrees with a separate height() function and add them. The answer is the largest sum, so also look inside the left and right subtrees.

  • height(node) = number of nodes on the longest path down (0 for an empty child).
  • A path bending at a node goes down height(left) edges on one side and height(right) on the other.
Time O(n²) worst case Space O(h) call stack

The same heights get worked out again and again. On a 10⁴-node chain it took 7.4 s in Python here (about 0.4 s in C++ and 0.3 s in Java); on a balanced tree it's only O(n log n).

Approach 2: One DFS That Returns Heights Optimal

A node's height needs its children's heights first, which is exactly what the bend check needs too. So do both in one post-order DFS: get left and right, update best with left + right, and return 1 + max(left, right).

  • The function returns a height but the answer is a path: keep the answer in a separate variable.
  • A path can't go down both sides of a node and then continue up, which is why the parent only gets max(left, right), not the sum.
Time O(n) Space O(h) call stack

Every node is visited once. The Python version raises the recursion limit, because a chain of 10⁴ nodes is 10⁴ calls deep. The same "return one thing, track another" DFS solves Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum and Balanced Binary Tree.

Approach 3: Iterative Post-Order with a Stack

The same post-order work without recursion. Each node goes on the stack twice: first to push its children, then (marked "back") to finish it once both children have heights.

  • Push (node, true), then the right child, then the left: the stack is last-in, first-out, so the left side runs first and the node finishes last.
  • A map holds each finished node's height, with an empty child counted as 0.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

No recursion limit to worry about, at the cost of a height map for every node. Useful when a tree can be very deep.

In practice No shortcut

LeetCode's TreeNode is a bare class, so there's no library function for a tree's diameter. Graph libraries (like NetworkX's diameter) would need the tree turned into a graph first.

Write Approach 2. The pattern to remember: when the answer at a node combines both children but the parent only needs one of them, return one value and keep the answer in a variable.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Brute Force height(left) + height(right) at every node O(n²) O(h) Recomputes heights; 7.4 s in Python on a 10⁴ chain
One DFS That Returns Heights Post-order; return height, track best O(n) O(h) Expected answer
Iterative Post-Order Stack of (node, back?) and a height map O(n) O(n) No recursion depth limit
572. Subtree of Another Tree Easy Tree DFS String Matching
Key idea: A subtree means a node and everything below it. Try each node of root as the top and ask "is this the same tree as subRoot?", where same means equal values and both trees end (None) in the same places. That's O(m·n). For O(m + n), write both trees in preorder with a marker for every missing child and search for one list inside the other.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the roots of two binary trees, root and subRoot, return true if some node of root, together with all of its descendants, has exactly the same structure and values as subRoot. A tree counts as a subtree of itself.

  • root has 1 to 2000 nodes; subRoot has 1 to 1000.
  • -10⁴ <= Node.val <= 10⁴.

Examples: root = [3,4,5,1,2], subRoot = [4,1,2] → true; root = [3,4,5,1,2,null,null,null,null,0], same subRoot → false (the 4 there has an extra 0 below it).

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

root / subRoot Expected Why it's tricky
[3,4,5,1,2,null,null,null,null,0] / [4,1,2] false The 4 matches until its 2, which has a 0 below it. A same() that returns true as soon as subRoot runs out says true.
[1,2,3] / [1,2] false subRoot is the top part of root, not a subtree: root's 1 also has a 3. Same mistake, same wrong true.
[1,2] / [1,null,2] false Left child vs right child. Without markers for missing children, both preorders are 1, 2.
[12] / [2] false As strings, "12,#,#" contains "2,#,#". Put a separator before each value too: ",12,#,#" doesn't contain ",2,#,#".
[1,1] / [1] true The root 1 fails (it has a child), but its child 1 is a leaf and matches. Keep looking after a failure.
[1,2,null,3] / [3] true The match is two levels down. Calling same() on root's children instead of recursing only looks one level down and says false.
[1] / [1,1] false subRoot is bigger than root.

Approach 1: Same Tree at Every Node

Two helpers. same(a, b) walks both trees together: equal values, then same left subtrees, then same right subtrees; two Nones are the same, one None isn't. isSubtree asks same(node, subRoot) at root, then recurses into both children.

  • same() stops at the first difference, so most tries end quickly.
  • Recurse with isSubtree on the children (not same), so every node gets tried.
Time O(m · n) Space O(height) for the recursion

The answer most interviewers expect, and fast enough here: the worst input tried (a 2000-node chain of 1s against a 1000-node chain of 1s ending in 2) took 140 ms in Python and 10 ms in C++. Approaches 2 and 3 took about 1 ms on it.

Approach 2: Preorder Lists + KMP Optimal

Write each tree as its preorder list, with a marker (∅) for every missing child. With the markers, the list describes the tree exactly, and each subtree is one unbroken run of the list. So subRoot is a subtree exactly when its list appears inside root's list.

  • Keep the values as list items (or put a separator before each one), so 12 can't be mistaken for 2.
  • KMP finds the pattern in O(m + n): on a mismatch it falls back using fail[] and never re-reads the text.
  • A match must start at a value, and a subtree's list can't stop partway through another subtree, so a match is always a whole subtree.
Time O(m + n) Space O(m + n)

Linear in the worst case, and it uses no hashing. The cost is writing KMP correctly; the built-in string search below does the same job with less code.

Approach 3: Number Every Subtree

Give each distinct subtree a number, bottom up: empty is #0, and a node's number is looked up by the key (value, left #, right #). A key not seen before gets the next number. Two subtrees get the same number exactly when they're equal.

  • Number subRoot first; call its number target.
  • Then number root with the same table: true if any node gets target.
  • The numbers are exact, not hashes that might collide, so no double-check is needed.
Time O(m + n) with a hash map Space O(m + n)

The same numbering finds every pair of equal subtrees in one tree, as in Find Duplicate Subtrees (652). The C++ version here uses std::map, which adds a log factor.

In practice Built-ins

Approach 2 with the language's own substring search: build a string with a "," before every value and "#" for every missing child, then use in (Python), find (C++), or indexOf (Java).

Time O(m + n) to build; the search is fast in practice Space O(m + n)

All three pass every test here, in a few milliseconds at most. The library searches don't all promise linear time in the worst case, so KMP is the version to explain if asked for a guarantee.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Same Tree at Every Node same(node, subRoot) everywhere O(m · n) O(height) Expected in interviews; 140 ms worst here
Preorder Lists + KMP Serialize with ∅, pattern search O(m + n) O(m + n) Linear guarantee
Number Every Subtree (value, left #, right #) → number O(m + n) O(m + n) Exact, no collisions
1448. Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree Medium Tree DFS BFS
Key idea: Walk down from the root carrying the largest value seen on the path so far. A node is good when node.val >= best; then pass max(best, node.val) to its children. Each path has its own maximum, so it's a parameter, not a global. O(n) time, O(h) space.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given the root of a binary tree, a node X is good if no node on the path from the root to X has a value greater than X. Return the number of good nodes.

  • The number of nodes is between 1 and 10⁵.
  • Each value is between -10⁴ and 10⁴.

Examples (level order, null = no child): [3, 1, 4, 3, null, 1, 5] → 4 (3, 4, 5 and the lower 3); [3, 3, null, 4, 2] → 3; [1] → 1.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[1] 1 One node: the root is always good.
[3, 3, null, 4, 2] 3 Equal counts as good: the second 3 is good. Use >=, not >.
[2, 2, 2, 2, 2] 5 All equal: every node is good.
[5, 1, null, 3] 1 3 is bigger than its parent 1, but not than 5 at the top. Compare with the largest value on the whole path, not just the parent.
[2, null, 4, 10, 8, null, null, 4] 4 Each path has its own maximum: 8 is good even though its sibling 10 is bigger. A single global maximum gets this wrong.
[-3, -2, -1] 3 Negative values: start best at root.val (or −∞). Starting at 0 counts nothing here.
[5, 4, null, 3, null, 2, null, 1] 1 A one-sided chain that only decreases: only the root is good.
[-10⁴, 10⁴, -10⁴] 3 Both limits: the root −10⁴ is good, and each child is ≥ it.
A chain 0 → 1 → … → 99999, each a left child 100000 10⁵ levels deep: recursion goes past Python's default limit of 1,000, and overflowed Java's default stack here. Raise the limit, or use a stack or queue.

Approach 1: Recursive DFS

The only thing a node needs from above is the largest value on its path. Pass it down as a parameter: each call checks its own node, then hands max(best, node.val) to both children.

  • dfs(node, best) returns the number of good nodes in that subtree: 1 if node.val >= best, plus the counts from the left and right subtrees.
  • Starting with best = root.val makes the root good and handles negative values. A starting value of 0 would not.
Time O(n) Space O(h)

h is the tree's height: about log n when balanced, up to n = 10⁵ when it's a single chain. Python raises its recursion limit here (default 1,000); with that, a 10⁵-deep chain passed in testing. C++ handled it too with a normal build. Java's recursive version threw StackOverflowError on that chain with the default JVM stack on this machine. LeetCode's JVM settings may differ, but Approach 2 avoids the question.

Approach 2: Iterative DFS with a Stack

The same walk, with your own stack instead of the call stack. Each entry is a pair: a node and the largest value above it. That pair is exactly what the recursive call had in its parameters.

  • Pop a pair, count the node if it's good, then push its children with max(best, node.val).
  • Pushing right before left makes left come out first, the same order as the recursion. For counting, any order works.
Time O(n) Space O(h)

The stack lives on the heap, so a 10⁵-deep tree is fine in every language. In Java, two stacks kept in step avoid creating a pair object per node.

Approach 3: BFS with a Queue

Visit level by level with a queue of (node, largest value above it). Because every entry carries its own path's maximum, it doesn't matter that nodes from different branches are mixed together.

  • Same check and same max(best, node.val) for the children; only the order of visits changes.
  • The queue holds about one level at a time, so memory follows the tree's width instead of its height.
Time O(n) Space O(w)

w is the widest level: up to about n / 2 for a full tree, 1 for a chain. Choose BFS when the tree is likely deep and narrow, DFS when it's wide and shallow; for this problem both pass easily.

In practice No shortcut

None of the standard libraries have a binary tree type with a traversal built in, and LeetCode's TreeNode is a bare class. A traversal is the shortest correct answer.

Approach 1 is the one to write: about six lines and the clearest. If the tree can be very deep (or in Java), use Approach 2.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Recursive DFS Pass the path maximum down as a parameter O(n) O(h) Shortest; deep trees can overflow the call stack
Iterative DFS with a Stack Stack of (node, max above it) O(n) O(h) Safe for 10⁵-deep trees in any language
BFS with a Queue Queue of (node, max above it), level by level O(n) O(w) Memory follows the width, not the height
Heap / Priority Queue 5 problems Always pop the smallest (or biggest) first
215. Kth Largest Element in an Array Medium Heap (Priority Queue) Quickselect Sorting
Key idea: You don't need the whole array sorted. A min-heap of size k keeps the k biggest values, and its top is the answer: O(n log k). Quickselect does better on average: split around a random pivot and keep only the side that holds the answer, O(n). Split into three parts (bigger, equal, smaller) so repeated values don't slow it down.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Return the k-th largest value in nums: the k-th in sorted order, counting repeats (not the k-th distinct value). LeetCode asks for a solution without sorting.

  • 1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10⁵
  • -10⁴ <= nums[i] <= 10⁴

Example: [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2 → 5. [3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6], k = 4 → 4.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
10⁵ copies of 1, k = 50000 1 Quickselect with a 2-way split moves only one value per round when all are equal: 1.2 s in C++. The 3-way split took 0.07 ms.
[3,2,3,1,2,4,5,5,6], k = 4 4 Repeats count: the order is 6, 5, 5, 4. Removing duplicates first gives 3.
[1], k = 1 1 One value.
[2,1], k = 2 1 k = n is the smallest value: watch the off-by-one (index k − 1 from the top).

Approach 1: Sort

Sort, biggest first, and return index k − 1 (or sort ascending and take index n − k).

  • Two lines, and hard to get wrong.
  • It orders everything, which this problem doesn't need, and LeetCode asks you not to.
Time O(n log n) Space O(n) in Python, O(log n) in place

10⁵ random values: Python 10.9 ms, Java 4.7 ms, C++ 1.7 ms. In Python this is the fastest of the three, because the sort runs in C.

Approach 2: Min-Heap of Size k

Push each value into a min-heap. When it holds more than k, pop the smallest. At the end it holds the k biggest values, and the top is the smallest of those: the answer.

  • Works on a stream: you never need all of nums at once.
  • Fast for small k; slow when k is about n / 2.
Time O(n log k) Space O(k)

10⁵ random values, k = 50000: Python 30 ms, Java 9.5 ms, C++ 3.7 ms, the slowest here in every language.

Approach 3: Quickselect, 3-Way Split Optimal

Pick a random pivot and split the values into bigger, equal and smaller. If k falls in the bigger part, keep only that; if it falls on the equal part, the pivot is the answer; otherwise keep the smaller part and subtract what you skipped from k.

  • Each round keeps one side, so the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n on average.
  • The random pivot means no fixed input is always slow. The worst case is still O(n²), but it's very unlikely.
  • C++ and Java split in place (Dutch national flag); Python builds lists for clarity.
Time O(n) average, O(n²) worst Space O(1) in place (O(n) for Python's lists)

10⁵ random values: Java 1.2 ms, C++ 0.84 ms, the fastest written-out solution in both. Python 11.5 ms, about the same as sorting.

In practice Built-ins

C++ has std::nth_element, a quickselect that puts the k-th value in its sorted place. Python has heapq.nlargest(k, nums), which keeps a size-k heap. Java has neither, so use Approach 2 or 3.

Time O(n) average (C++), O(n log k) (Python) Space O(1) (C++), O(k) (Python)

Should pass on LeetCode. nth_element took 0.69 ms on 10⁵ values, the fastest here. heapq.nlargest took 56 ms with k = 50000: for a big k, sorted is faster in Python.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Sort Sort, read index k − 1 O(n log n) O(n) Fastest in Python
Min-Heap of Size k Keep the k biggest O(n log k) O(k) Good for streams and small k
Quickselect, 3-Way Split Random pivot, keep one side O(n) average O(1) Fastest in C++ and Java
295. Find Median from Data Stream Hard Heap (Priority Queue) Design Data Stream
Key idea: Split the values into two halves: low, a max-heap of the smaller half, and high, a min-heap of the bigger half. Keep every value in low ≤ every value in high, and low's size equal to high's or one more. The median is low's top, or the mean of both tops. O(log n) per add, O(1) per find.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Build MedianFinder with addNum(num) and findMedian(), which returns the median of all values so far: the middle value, or the mean of the two middle values when the count is even.

  • -10⁵ <= num <= 10⁵; at most 5 × 10⁴ calls in total
  • findMedian is only called after at least one addNum

Example: add 1, add 2, find → 1.5; add 3, find → 2.0.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
add 95423, −53162, −46989, find -46989.0 Putting each value into whichever heap is smaller, without passing it through the other, breaks "low ≤ high": it said 95423.0. Wrong on 1482 of 2004 tests.
add 12633, −62910, find -25138.5 Integer division for the mean rounds down: it said -25139.0. Wrong on 1213 tests.
add −100000, 100000, find 0.0 The two middles cancel out.

Approach 1: Sort on Every Find

addNum appends. findMedian sorts a copy of everything and reads the middle.

  • Fine if you add a lot and ask rarely.
  • Terrible if you ask after every add.
Time O(1) add, O(n log n) find Space O(n)

25,000 adds, each followed by a find: C++ 5.3 s, Java 28 s (Python wasn't even tried). But 5 × 10⁴ adds and one find: C++ 1.1 ms, Python 10 ms, the fastest here.

Approach 2: Sorted List, Binary Insert

Keep the list sorted: binary search for the spot and insert there. findMedian just reads the middle.

  • The search is O(log n), but inserting shifts everything after it.
Time O(n) add, O(1) find Space O(n)

5 × 10⁴ adds and one find: Python 321 ms, Java 62 ms, C++ 43 ms. Find after every add (25,000 each): Python 93 ms, C++ 13 ms.

Approach 3: Two Heaps Optimal

To add: push into low, then move low's biggest into high. That keeps every low value ≤ every high value. If high now has more, move its smallest back to low. To find: low's top if low is bigger, else the mean of both tops.

  • Python's heapq is only a min-heap, so low stores negated values.
  • Use floating-point division for the mean.
Time O(log n) add, O(1) find Space O(n)

Find after every add (25,000 each): Python 26 ms, Java 13 ms, C++ 2.4 ms, the fastest in every language for that pattern.

In practice No shortcut

Python's statistics.median sorts the whole list each call, like Approach 1. Outside LeetCode, the sortedcontainers package's SortedList makes Approach 2 O(log n) per add.

On LeetCode, Approach 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Sort on Every Find Append; sort when asked O(1) / O(n log n) O(n) 28 s in Java when asked often
Sorted List, Binary Insert Insert at the right spot O(n) / O(1) O(n) Shifting is the cost
Two Heaps Max-heap low, min-heap high O(log n) / O(1) O(n) Expected answer
347. Top K Frequent Elements Medium Heap Bucket Sort Hash Map
Key idea: Count each value. A count is at most n, so put each value in bucket[count] and read the buckets from the top until you have k. O(n), no sort. A size-k min-heap (O(n log k)) is the other common answer.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Return the k values that appear most often in nums, in any order. The answer is promised to be unique.

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 10⁵, -10⁴ <= nums[i] <= 10⁴
  • k is between 1 and the number of different values
  • Follow-up: better than O(n log n).

Example: nums = [1,1,1,2,2,3], k = 2 → [1,2]. nums = [1], k = 1 → [1].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
nums = [1], k = 1 [1] A value can appear n times, so the buckets need slots 0 to n. With only n buckets this crashed with an IndexError on 184 of 3,006 tests.
nums = [-1,-1,2], k = 2 [-1,2] Negative values: count with a hash map, not an array indexed by value.
10⁵ different values plus one repeat, k = 1 the repeated value Almost every bucket is empty, but the bucket loop still only walks n + 1 of them.

Approach 1: Count, Then Sort

Count each value in a hash map. Sort the different values by count, biggest first, and return the first k.

  • Simple. Doesn't meet the follow-up when most values are different.
Time O(n log n) Space O(n)

10⁵ numbers, about 20,000 different values, average of 30 runs: Python 9.6 ms, Java 5.0 ms, C++ 2.7 ms. The fastest of the three in Python, because sorted runs in C.

Approach 2: Size-k Min-Heap

After counting, push each value into a min-heap keyed by count. When the heap holds more than k, pop the top: it's the least frequent of them. The k left are the answer.

  • Good when k is small. Also works on a stream of counts.
Time O(n log k) Space O(n) for the counts, O(k) for the heap

Same input, k = 10: Python 12 ms, Java 4.0 ms, C++ 2.6 ms. With k = 4689: Python 18.5 ms, Java 8.3 ms, C++ 4.0 ms, the slowest of the three.

Approach 3: Bucket by Count Optimal

A count is between 1 and n. Make n + 1 buckets and put each value in bucket[count]. Walk the buckets from n down, taking values until you have k.

  • No comparisons between counts at all.
Time O(n) Space O(n)

Same input: Java 3.2 ms and C++ 2.6 ms, the fastest for both ks (in C++ only just: counting takes most of the time). Python 17 ms, behind Approach 1: building 10⁵ + 1 lists in Python costs more than a sort in C.

In practice Built-ins

Python's Counter(nums).most_common(k) counts in C and then uses heapq.nlargest, which is Approach 2. C++ and Java have no one-liner; use Approach 3.

Time O(n log k) Space O(n)

Should pass on LeetCode. Same input: 5.1 ms with k = 10, the fastest Python here. 10.9 ms with k = 4689, a bit behind Approach 1.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Count, Then Sort Sort values by count O(n log n) O(n) Fastest in Python
Size-k Min-Heap Drop the least frequent past k O(n log k) O(n) Slows as k grows
Bucket by Count bucket[count], read from the top O(n) O(n) Expected answer
355. Design Twitter Medium Heap Design Hash Map
Key idea: Keep each user's tweets in posting order with a time stamp. A feed is "merge k sorted lists", stopped after 10: put each followed user's newest tweet in a max-heap, pop the newest, and push that user's next older tweet. O(F + 10 log F) per feed.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Build a Twitter class:

  • postTweet(userId, tweetId): the user posts a new tweet. Tweet ids are unique.
  • getNewsFeed(userId): the 10 most recent tweet ids posted by the user or anyone they follow, newest first.
  • follow(followerId, followeeId) and unfollow(followerId, followeeId).
  • 1 <= userId <= 500, 0 <= tweetId <= 10⁴, at most 3·10⁴ calls in all.

Example: post(1, 5), feed(1) → [5], follow(1, 2), post(2, 6), feed(1) → [6, 5], unfollow(1, 2), feed(1) → [5].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
post(2, 1), feed(2) [1] The feed includes your own tweets. Reading only the users you follow was wrong on 1,137 of 1,504 tests.
unfollow(1, 2) before any follow nothing happens Python's set.remove raises a KeyError here; use discard. With remove, 1,175 of 1,504 tests crashed.
12 posts by user 1, then feed(1) the last 10, newest first Stop at 10.

Approach 1: One Global List

Append every (user, tweet) to one list. For a feed, walk it from the newest end and keep tweets by the user or anyone they follow, stopping at 10.

  • No clock needed: the list order is the time order.
  • Fast when the newest tweets are the ones you want. Slow for a user whose tweets are old: the scan passes everyone else's.
Time post O(1), feed O(T) for T tweets Space O(T + follows)

15,000 feeds for a user whose one tweet is behind 15,000 others': Python 8.2 s, Java 0.53 s, C++ 0.11 s. 3·10⁴ random calls over 500 users: Python 260 ms, 6 times Approach 3.

Approach 2: Gather and Sort

Keep tweets per user, each with a time stamp. For a feed, take the last 10 tweets of the user and of each followed user (older ones can never make the top 10), sort them newest first, and keep 10.

  • The "last 10" cut keeps a feed from depending on how much anyone has posted.
Time post O(1), feed O(10F log(10F)) for F followed users Space O(T + follows)

A user following 499 busy users, 14,500 feeds: Python 14.4 s, Java 4.7 s, C++ 1.8 s, the slowest here. It sorts about 5,000 tweets for every feed.

Approach 3: Merge With a Heap Optimal

Each user's tweets are already sorted by time. Put every followed user's newest tweet in a max-heap by time. Pop the newest into the feed and push that user's next older tweet. Stop after 10 pops.

  • The same merge as 23. Merge k Sorted Lists, cut off at 10.
Time post O(1), feed O(F + 10 log F) Space O(T + follows)

3·10⁴ random calls: Python 41 ms, Java 18 ms, C++ 5.5 ms, the fastest in every language. Following 499 users: Python 1.6 s, Java 0.31 s, C++ 0.061 s, 9 to 30 times faster than Approach 2. Approach 1 was faster still there (C++ 2.3 ms) because the newest 10 tweets were all in the feed.

In practice No shortcut

Nothing built in. Python's heapq.merge could replace the hand-written merge in Approach 3. Real feed systems usually do the work when tweets are posted (fan-out on write) instead of on every read.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
One Global List Scan every tweet from the newest Feed O(T) O(T) 8.2 s worst case in Python
Gather and Sort Last 10 of each user, sorted Feed O(10F log(10F)) O(T) Slow with many follows
Merge With a Heap Merge k sorted lists, stop at 10 Feed O(F + 10 log F) O(T) Expected answer
703. Kth Largest Element in a Stream Easy Heap (Priority Queue) Design Data Stream
Key idea: Only the k biggest values ever matter. Keep them in a min-heap of size k: push each new value, and if the heap has more than k, pop the smallest. The top is the k-th biggest. O(log k) per add, O(k) memory.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Build KthLargest(k, nums). Each add(val) adds a value to the stream and returns the k-th largest value so far (counting repeats).

  • 0 <= nums.length <= 10⁴, 1 <= k <= nums.length + 1
  • At most 10⁴ calls to add; values are in [-10⁴, 10⁴]

Example: k = 3, nums = [4,5,8,2], then add 3, 5, 10, 9, 4 → 4, 5, 5, 8, 8.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
k = 1, nums = [], add 8140, 2362 8140, 8140 A min-heap that never trims back to k returns the smallest value instead: 8140, 2362. Wrong on 1944 of 2004 tests.
k = 1, nums = [] - The stream starts empty; the first add brings it to k values.
k = 4, nums = [7,7,7,7,8,3], add 2 7 Repeats count: the top four are 8, 7, 7, 7.

Approach 1: Sort on Every Add

Keep every value. On each add, append it, sort everything biggest first, and return position k − 1.

  • Memory keeps growing with the stream.
  • Python's sort (Timsort) finds the already-sorted run, so re-sorting after one append took 51 µs for 20,000 values, against 1.8 ms for a random list.
Time O(n log n) per add (less with Timsort) Space O(n)

10⁴ starting values, then 10⁴ adds, k = 5000: Python 450 ms, Java 197 ms, C++ 206 ms.

Approach 2: Sorted List, Binary Insert

Sort the starting values once. For each add, binary search for where the value goes and insert it there. The answer is the k-th value from the end.

  • The search is O(log n), but inserting shifts everything after it: O(n).
Time O(n) per add Space O(n)

Same test: Python 43 ms, Java 12 ms, C++ 9.4 ms.

Approach 3: Min-Heap of Size k Optimal

Push each value (starting ones too) into a min-heap, and pop whenever it holds more than k. What stays is the k biggest; the top is the smallest of them, which is the answer.

  • Values that are popped can never come back into the top k, so throwing them away is safe.
Time O(log k) per add Space O(k)

Same test: Python 6.9 ms, Java 3.6 ms, C++ 1.8 ms, the fastest in every language. With k = 1: C++ 0.15 ms.

In practice No shortcut

Approach 3 already uses the built-in heaps (heapq, priority_queue, PriorityQueue). That's what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Sort on Every Add Append and sort O(n log n) per add O(n) Memory keeps growing
Sorted List, Binary Insert Insert at the right spot O(n) per add O(n) Shifting is the cost
Min-Heap of Size k Keep the k biggest O(log k) per add O(k) Expected answer
Tries 3 problems A tree of letters, one child per next letter
208. Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) Medium Trie Design Hash Table
Key idea: A trie is a tree of letters. Each node has one child per next letter, and a flag that says "a word ends here". Inserting or looking up a word of length L walks L nodes, so startsWith costs O(L) no matter how many words are stored. search must also check the end flag.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Build a Trie class with insert(word), search(word) (was this exact word inserted?) and startsWith(prefix) (does any inserted word start with it?).

  • 1 <= word.length, prefix.length <= 2000, lowercase letters only
  • At most 3 × 10⁴ calls in total

Example: insert("apple"), search("apple") → true, search("app") → false, startsWith("app") → true, insert("app"), search("app") → true.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
insert("apple"), search("app") false "app" is only a prefix. A search that doesn't check the end flag says true.
then insert("app"), search("app") true Inserting a word that's a prefix of another adds no nodes: it only sets the end flag.
10,000 inserts, then 20,000 searches and prefix checks - A plain set has to scan every word for startsWith: 3.2 s in Python.
a 2000-letter word - 2000 nodes in one chain. Fine for a loop; a recursive insert would go 2000 calls deep.

Approach 1: Hash Set of Words

Keep the words in a set. insert and search are one hash operation each. startsWith has no shortcut: check whether any stored word starts with the prefix.

  • Fine if prefix checks are rare.
  • startsWith costs O(total letters stored).
Time O(L) insert/search, O(N·L) startsWith Space O(total letters)

10,000 words, then 20,000 mixed queries: Python 3.2 s, Java 692 ms, C++ 236 ms. About 45 to 190 times slower than a trie.

Approach 2: Trie of Hash Maps

Each node is a map from letter to child. insert walks the letters, adding missing nodes, and marks the last node as a word end. A shared walk finds the node for a string; search also needs the end mark, startsWith doesn't.

  • Nodes only store the letters they use: good for big alphabets.
  • In Python a node is just a dict, with "$" as the end mark.
Time O(L) per call Space O(total letters)

Same 30,000 calls: Python 20 ms, the fastest in Python. Java 6.6 ms, C++ 5.2 ms.

Approach 3: Trie With 26 Child Slots Optimal

Only lowercase letters appear, so each node can hold an array of 26 children: the child for ch is at ch − 'a'. No hashing, just an index.

  • The usual interview answer, and the fastest in C++ and Java.
  • Each node holds 26 slots even if it uses one, so it takes more memory.
Time O(L) per call Space O(26 · nodes)

Same 30,000 calls: Java 3.6 ms, C++ 3.1 ms. Python 35 ms: slower than Approach 2 here. In Python, a small dict per node beat a 26-slot list.

In practice No shortcut

The standard libraries have no trie. With a sorted list of words, a binary search (bisect, lower_bound, TreeSet.ceiling) finds the first word ≥ the prefix, and checking that one word answers startsWith.

For this problem, Approach 2 or 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Hash Set of Words Scan every word for a prefix O(N·L) startsWith O(total letters) 3.2 s in Python
Trie of Hash Maps letter → child map per node O(L) O(total letters) Fastest in Python
Trie With 26 Child Slots child[ch − 'a'] O(L) O(26 · nodes) Fastest in C++ and Java
211. Design Add and Search Words Data Structure Medium Trie Design Depth-First Search
Key idea: Store the words in a trie. Search with a DFS over the pattern: a letter follows its one child, a "." tries every child, and a match must end on a node marked as a word end. Words that don't share the pattern's letters are never looked at.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Build WordDictionary with addWord(word) and search(word). In search, each "." matches any one letter. Return whether some added word matches.

  • 1 <= word.length <= 25; added words are lowercase letters
  • A search has at most 2 dots; at most 10⁴ calls in total

Example: add bad, dad, mad. search("pad") → false, search("bad") → true, search(".ad") → true, search("b..") → true.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
add ab, cd; search(".d") true A "." must try every child. Returning the result of the first child only said false; wrong on 414 of 2001 tests.
add bad; search("ba") false The letters match but "ba" isn't a word: check the end flag.
add a; search(".") true A pattern that's only a dot.
5000 words of length 25, then 5000 searches starting with ".." all false The list and the length groups compare every word: 11 s+ in Python. The trie takes 0.94 s.

Approach 1: List of Words

Keep every word in a list. To search, compare the pattern with each word of the same length, letter by letter, letting "." match anything.

  • The simplest to write, and addWord is O(1).
  • Every search can touch every word.
Time O(N·L) per search Space O(total letters)

5000 words of length 25, then 5000 ".." searches: Python 11.3 s, Java 93 ms, C++ 87 ms. Even exact searches took 1.2 s in Python.

Approach 2: Group by Length

Only words of the same length can match, so keep a set per length. A search without "." is one hash lookup. A search with dots scans just its length group.

  • The fastest for exact searches: 2.8 ms for 5000 in Python.
  • But if all words have the same length, a dotted search still checks them all.
Time O(L) exact, O(N·L) with dots Space O(total letters)

The ".." test above: Python 11.8 s, Java 226 ms, C++ 120 ms, no better than Approach 1, because every word has length 25.

Approach 3: Trie With DFS Optimal

addWord is a normal trie insert. dfs(node, i) asks whether word[i:] can be spelled from node: at the end, check the end flag; on a letter, follow that one child; on ".", try every child and stop at the first success.

  • Shared prefixes are walked once, and wrong letters cut whole branches.
  • With at most 2 dots, a search visits at most 26² branches.
  • The Python version uses dict children: in Implement Trie, dicts were faster than 26-slot lists in Python.
Time O(L) letters, up to O(26ᵈ·L) with d dots Space O(total letters)

The ".." test: Python 0.94 s, Java 37 ms, C++ 27 ms, 12 times faster than Approach 1 in Python. For exact searches, Approach 2 was faster (2.8 ms vs 15 ms in Python).

In practice No shortcut

re.fullmatch(pattern, word) treats "." the same way, but it still has to be run on every word. No standard library has a trie.

Approach 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
List of Words Compare with every word O(N·L) O(total letters) 11.3 s in Python
Group by Length Set per length O(L) exact, O(N·L) dots O(total letters) Best for exact searches
Trie With DFS "." tries every child O(26ᵈ·L) O(total letters) Expected answer
212. Word Search II Hard Trie Backtracking Matrix
Key idea: Don't search the board once per word. Put all the words in a trie and run one DFS from every cell, walking the board and the trie together: a path stops as soon as no word continues with its letters. Clear each found word, and cut trie branches that have nothing left.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Given a board of letters and a list of words, return every word that can be spelled by a path of cells joined up, down, left or right, using each cell at most once per word. Any order.

  • 1 <= m, n <= 12, lowercase letters
  • 1 <= words.length <= 3 × 10⁴, each 1 to 10 letters, all different

Example: board ["oaan","etae","ihkr","iflv"], words ["oath","pea","eat","rain"] → ["eat","oath"]. Board ["ab","cd"], words ["abcb"] → [].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
board ["a","a"], words ["aa"] ["aa"] Two paths spell it. Not clearing a found word from the trie reported it twice; wrong on 1204 of 1505 tests.
board ["a","b"], words ["ab","ba"] both Forgetting to unmark a cell on the way back blocks it for later paths: only "ab" was found.
board ["ab","cd"], words ["abcb"] [] The second b would reuse a cell.
12 × 12 of a, words a…aaaaaaaaaa and aaaaaaaaa + each other letter the 10 all-a words Every path of as matches a prefix. Searching per word took 23 s in Python; the pruned trie, 0.56 s.

Approach 1: Word Search for Each Word

Reuse Word Search (79): for each word, try every cell as the start and DFS letter by letter, marking cells on the path and unmarking them on the way back. Keep the words that are found.

  • Correct, and fine for a handful of words.
  • Words that share a prefix redo the same walks, and the board is scanned once per word.
Time O(W · m·n · 3ᴸ) Space O(L) call stack

All-a board, 35 words: Python 23 s, Java 268 ms, C++ 174 ms. A random 12 × 12 board with 3000 words: Python 75 ms.

Approach 2: Trie + DFS From Every Cell

Build a trie of all the words. From each cell, DFS while following the trie: a step is only taken if the trie has a child for that cell's letter. When a node holds a word, add it to the answer and clear it.

  • One walk checks all words with that prefix at once.
  • Marking the cell with "#" also stops the DFS, because no trie node has a "#" child.
Time O(m·n · 3ᴸ) Space O(total letters in words)

All-a board: Python 1.4 s, Java 24 ms, C++ 22 ms, 17 times faster than Approach 1 in Python. Random board, 3000 words: Python 6.1 ms.

Approach 3: Trie + DFS + Pruning Optimal

Same as Approach 2, plus one step on the way back: if the child node now has no word and no children, delete it from its parent. Branches whose words are all found disappear, and later paths stop earlier.

  • C++ and Java keep a child count per node, so the "empty?" check is O(1).
  • The more words are found, the smaller the trie gets.
Time O(m·n · 3ᴸ) at worst, much less in practice Space O(total letters in words)

All-a board: Python 0.56 s, Java 9.3 ms, C++ 8.9 ms, 2.5 times faster than Approach 2. Random board: the same as Approach 2 (few words are found, so little is cut).

In practice No shortcut

No library walks a board for you, and none has a trie. Approach 3 is what you'd write.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Word Search for Each Word One board search per word O(W · m·n · 3ᴸ) O(L) 23 s in Python on the all-a board
Trie + DFS Walk board and trie together O(m·n · 3ᴸ) O(letters) Clear found words
Trie + DFS + Pruning Also cut empty branches O(m·n · 3ᴸ) O(letters) Expected answer
Graphs 14 problems BFS, level by level
127. Word Ladder Hard Hash Table String BFS
Key idea: Words are nodes, and two words are joined if they differ by one letter. The shortest ladder is a BFS from beginWord. Find neighbors by changing each letter to a…z and looking the result up in a set, and remove a word from the set as soon as it's queued. Searching from both ends at once is faster still.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

A ladder goes from beginWord to endWord, changing one letter at a time. Every word after the first must be in wordList (beginWord itself doesn't have to be). Return the number of words in the shortest ladder, or 0 if there is none.

  • 1 <= beginWord.length <= 10; endWord and every word in wordList have the same length
  • 1 <= wordList.length <= 5000
  • Lowercase letters only; beginWord != endWord; the words in wordList are unique

Example: "hit" → "cog" with ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"] → 5 (hit → hot → dot → dog → cog). Without "cog" in the list → 0.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
"hit", "cog", ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log"] 0 endWord isn't in the list. A two-ended search that skips this check starts its back side at "cog" anyway and said 5 here.
"hit", "cog", ["hot","dot","dog","lot","log","cog"] 5 Count the words, not the moves. Starting the count at 0 says 4.
"hit", "hot", ["hot"] 2 One change: the shortest possible ladder.
"a", "c", ["a","b","c"] 2 One-letter words: every word is next to every other. beginWord is in the list too; don't visit it again.
"hot", "dog", ["hot","dog"] 0 endWord is in the list but two letters away, with nothing in between.
"hot", "dog", ["hot","dot","dog"] 3 The list holds beginWord. Remove it from the set first, or it can be queued again later.
5,000 words of length 10, endWord with no neighbors 0 A one-way BFS visits every reachable word before giving up. The two-ended search stops at once: its back side is empty after one level.
5,000 words of length 10, about 12 neighbors each 9 Comparing each queued word with every unused word came to 7.2 million comparisons; Python took 2.7 s here.

Approach 1: BFS, Comparing With Every Word

BFS from beginWord, one level per extra word. For each word taken from the queue, compare it letter by letter with every word not used yet; the ones that differ in exactly one place join the queue.

  • BFS finds the shortest ladder because it reaches every word with the fewest steps first.
  • Mark a word used when it's queued, not when it's taken out, so it's never in the queue twice.
Time O(n² · L) Space O(n · L)

n = number of words, L = word length. Each word is compared with up to n others. Measured here on 5,000 words of length 10: Python 2.7 s, Java 0.2 s, C++ 71 ms. Fine when the words are long and few; slow when there are many short ones.

Approach 2: BFS, Trying Every One-Letter Change

Instead of comparing with all n words, make the neighbors: change each of the L letters to each of a…z and check whether the result is in a set of unused words. That's 26 · L lookups per word, no matter how long the list is.

  • Removing a word from the set when it's queued doubles as the "used" mark.
  • Marking it only when it comes out of the queue still gives the right answer, but the same word gets queued many times: 28,691 pushes instead of 4,960 on the 5,000-word test.
  • In C++ and Java, change the letter in place and put it back, instead of building a new string for every try.
Time O(n · 26 · L²) Space O(n · L)

26 · L tries per word, each costing O(L) to build and hash. On the same 5,000 words: Python 0.2 s (13× faster than Approach 1), Java 36 ms, C++ 13 ms. The standard interview answer.

Approach 3: Two-Ended BFS Optimal

Grow one level from beginWord and one from endWord, taking turns, and stop when a new word is already on the other side. Always grow the smaller side.

  • If each word has about d neighbors and the ladder has k steps, a one-way BFS looks at about dk words. Two searches that meet in the middle look at about 2 · dk/2.
  • Keep the endWord check: without it, the back side starts at a word that isn't allowed.
  • Swapping to the smaller side is what makes it fast: without the swap it took 192 ms here instead of 26 ms in Python.
Time O(n · 26 · L²) worst case Space O(n · L)

Same worst case as Approach 2, but far less work in practice. On the 5,000 words: Python 25 ms (8× faster than Approach 2), Java 15 ms, C++ 6 ms. When endWord has no neighbors, it stops after one level (0 ms vs 0.2 s). A strong follow-up after Approach 2.

In practice No shortcut

Python, C++ and Java have no shortest-path helper for this. The parts that matter are the set (set, unordered_set, HashSet) and the queue (deque, std::queue, ArrayDeque), both used above.

Approach 2 is what you'd write first; switch to Approach 3 when the list is large or the ladders are long.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
BFS, Comparing With Every Word Compare each queued word with all unused words O(n² · L) O(n · L) 2.7 s in Python at 5,000 words
BFS, Trying Every One-Letter Change 26 · L set lookups per word O(n · 26 · L²) O(n · L) Standard answer; mark words when queued
Two-Ended BFS Grow the smaller side until they meet O(n · 26 · L²) worst O(n · L) 8× faster than Approach 2 here; check endWord first
130. Surrounded Regions Medium Matrix BFS Union Find
Key idea: Flip the question around. Instead of asking which O's are surrounded, find the ones that aren't: start from every O on the border and mark everything connected to it as safe. Every O left unmarked is surrounded, so flip it. One pass, O(m · n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

board is a grid of 'X' and 'O'. A region is a group of O's joined up, down, left or right. A region is surrounded if none of its cells is on the edge of the board. Change every surrounded region to X, in place.

  • 1 <= m, n <= 200
  • board[i][j] is 'X' or 'O'

Example: XXXX / XOOX / XXOX / XOXX → XXXX / XXXX / XXXX / XOXX. The O at the bottom touches the edge, so it stays.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
XOX / XOX / XXX XOX / XOX / XXX The middle O isn't on the edge, but it connects to one that is. Flipping every inner O said XOX / XXX / XXX.
O O A 1 × 1 board: the only cell is on the edge.
OOO / OXO / OOO unchanged Every O is on the edge; nothing flips.
XXXXX / XOOOX / XOXOX / XOOOX / XXXXX all X A ring of O's with an X in the middle: the whole ring is surrounded.
200 × 200, one path of 19,701 O's zigzagging to the edge unchanged A recursive DFS goes 19,701 calls deep. Python's limit is 1,000: it raised RecursionError here. Use a queue or an explicit stack.
200 × 200, all O inside a ring of X all X One huge surrounded region. Searching it again from each of its 39,204 cells took 7.6 s in C++.

Approach 1: Search From Every O

For each O, run a fresh search through the O's next to it. If the search reaches the edge, the O stays; otherwise it's trapped. Flip the trapped ones at the end, after all the checks.

  • Simple, and each check is clearly right.
  • Wasteful: every O in a region searches that whole region again, so a region of k cells costs k².
Time O((m · n)²) Space O(m · n)

Measured on 200 × 200 boards. Random half-O: Python 0.6 s, C++ 0.12 s. One big surrounded region: C++ 7.6 s, Java 22 s. The zigzag path: Python 172 s, C++ 1.6 s. Far too slow at full size.

Approach 2: Spread From the Border (BFS) Optimal
