Approach 3 as a one-line fold: reduce(xor, nums) in Python, std::accumulate with std::bit_xor in C++, Arrays.stream(nums).reduce(0, (a, b) -> a ^ b) in Java.

Time O(n) Space O(1)

Same work as Approach 3: Python 1.0 ms, C++ 0.002 ms; the Java stream has some setup cost (6.2 ms). Another Python one-liner is 2 * sum(set(nums)) - sum(nums), which was right on 2,000 test arrays here, but builds a set, so it's O(n) memory.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Count With a Hash Map Count, find the 1 O(n) O(n) Breaks the memory rule
Sort, Then Check Pairs First pair that doesn't match O(n log n) O(1) extra Breaks the time rule
XOR Everything Pairs cancel; x ^ x = 0 O(n) O(1) Expected answer
202. Happy Number Easy Math Hash Table Two Pointers
Key idea: Replacing a number by the sum of the squares of its digits quickly gives small numbers, so the sequence must either reach 1 or repeat. Detect the repeat like a cycle in a linked list: slow takes one step, fast takes two, and they meet inside any loop. O(1) memory.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Start with n and keep replacing it with the sum of the squares of its digits. n is happy if this reaches 1. Return whether it's happy.

  • 1 <= n <= 2³¹ − 1

Example: 19 → true (1² + 9² = 82 → 68 → 100 → 1). 2 → false (2 → 4 → 16 → … → 4 again).

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
2 false A loop that only stops at 1 never ends: it goes 4, 16, 37, 58, 89, 145, 42, 20, 4, …
19 true Floyd's check with slow = fast = n at the start stops before moving and says false. Wrong on 441 of n = 1 to 2999.
7 true A one-digit number other than 1 can still be happy: 7 → 49 → 97 → 130 → 10 → 1. "Stop at one digit" was wrong for 7, 1112, 1121, …
1 true Already 1, no steps needed.

Approach 1: Hash Set

Remember every number you meet. If you reach 1, it's happy. If you meet a number a second time, the sequence is in a loop that doesn't contain 1.

  • Why it always ends: a number with d ≥ 4 digits goes to at most 81·d, which is smaller. So it soon drops below 1000, and then it has to repeat or hit 1.
Time O(log n) per step, few steps Space O(number of steps)

Average over 23,007 inputs: Python 5.7 µs, C++ 0.80 µs, Java 0.32 µs. In C++ the set costs more than the digit work.

Approach 2: Stop at 4

There is only one loop: 4 → 16 → 37 → 58 → 89 → 145 → 42 → 20 → 4. Every unhappy number falls into it, so loop until the number is 1 or 4.

  • Checked here: every n from 1 to 999 ends at 1 or in that loop, and bigger numbers always drop below 1000 first.
  • Fastest, but you have to know (or prove) the fact.
Time O(log n) per step Space O(1)

Average: Python 4.2 µs, C++ 0.10 µs, Java 0.15 µs, the fastest in every language.

Approach 3: Slow and Fast Pointers Optimal

Treat next(x) as a link, like a linked list. Start slow = n and fast = next(n). Each round, slow moves one step and fast two. If fast reaches 1, it's happy. If they meet, there's a loop without 1.

  • Start fast one step ahead (or move before checking), or the loop never runs.
  • No set and no special number: works without knowing the 4-loop fact.
Time O(log n) per step Space O(1)

Average: Python 6.1 µs, C++ 0.17 µs, Java 0.20 µs. Three next calls per round instead of one, and no memory.

In practice No shortcut

Nothing built in. Approach 1 is the easiest to explain; Approach 3 is the one interviewers usually look for.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Hash Set Stop on a repeat O(log n) per step O(steps) Simplest to explain
Stop at 4 The only loop contains 4 O(log n) per step O(1) Fastest; needs the fact
Slow and Fast Pointers Floyd's cycle check O(log n) per step O(1) Expected answer
Bit Manipulation 4 problems Shift, mask and count the bits
190. Reverse Bits Easy Bit Manipulation Divide and Conquer
Key idea: Move bits one at a time: 32 times, take n & 1, push it onto res with res = (res << 1) | bit, and shift n right. Always do all 32 rounds, even after n is 0, because the leading zeros of n become the trailing zeros of the answer.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Reverse the 32 bits of the integer n: bit 0 becomes bit 31, bit 1 becomes bit 30, and so on. Return the new number.

  • 0 <= n <= 2³¹ − 2, and n is even
  • Even means bit 0 is 0, so the answer's top bit is 0 and it fits in an int.

Example: 43261596 → 964176192. 2147483644 → 1073741822.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
2 1073741824 A loop that stops while n is non-zero runs only 2 rounds: it said 1. Wrong on all 10,004 inputs tried.
43261596 964176192 Reversing bin(n) without padding to 32 digits drops the leading zeros: it said 15065253.
0 0 No 1 bits at all.
2147483646 2147483646 31 ones then a 0: reversed, it's the same pattern. The biggest input.

Approach 1: Binary String, Reversed

Write n as exactly 32 binary digits, reverse the text, and parse it back in base 2.

  • The width 32 matters: the leading zeros are the bits that end up at the bottom.
  • It builds two 32-character strings each call.
Time O(1) (32 characters) Space O(1)

Average per call over 20,007 inputs: Python 0.47 µs (the fastest in Python, because the work happens inside C), C++ 0.28 µs, Java 0.65 µs, 6 to 13 times slower than the bit versions in C++ and Java.

Approach 2: Bit by Bit

32 rounds. Each round, n & 1 is the lowest bit of n. Shift res left and put that bit at its right end, then shift n right. The first bit taken ends up at the top after 31 more shifts.

  • Never stop early: the rounds after n becomes 0 are what move the bits up.
  • In Java use >>>, and in C++ an unsigned, so a shift never copies a sign bit.
Time O(1) (32 rounds) Space O(1)

Average per call: Python 2.6 µs (32 trips through the interpreter), Java 0.05 µs, C++ 0.05 µs. The answer most interviewers expect.

Approach 3: Swap Blocks With Masks Optimal

Reversing 32 bits is the same as swapping the two 16-bit halves and then reversing each half. Keep going: swap the bytes in each half, the 4-bit pieces in each byte, the pairs, and finally neighbouring bits. Each swap is one line: shift one way, shift the other, and keep the right blocks with a mask.

  • The masks are patterns: 0x55555555 is 0101…, 0x33333333 is 0011…, and so on.
  • 5 lines instead of 32 rounds: log₂ 32 = 5.
  • For the follow-up ("called many times"), a 256-entry table of reversed bytes is the other common answer.
Time O(1) (5 steps) Space O(1)

Average per call: Python 0.76 µs, Java 0.045 µs, C++ 0.04 µs, about the same as Approach 2 in C++ and Java. At this size the timer itself is a big part of what's measured.

In practice Built-ins

Java has Integer.reverse(n), which does the mask swaps of Approach 3 for you.

Time O(1) Space O(1)

Should pass on LeetCode (0.05 µs per call here). Python and C++ have no bit-reverse function. In Python, Approach 1 is the short way.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Binary String, Reversed Pad to 32 digits, reverse, parse O(1) O(1) Fastest in Python, slowest elsewhere
Bit by Bit 32 rounds of shift and OR O(1) O(1) Never stop when n hits 0
Swap Blocks With Masks Swap 16, 8, 4, 2, 1-bit blocks O(1) O(1) 5 lines, no loop
191. Number of 1 Bits Easy Bit Manipulation
Key idea: n & (n − 1) is n with its lowest 1 bit cleared. Repeat until n is 0 and count the rounds: the loop runs once per 1 bit, not once per bit position.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Return how many 1 bits the binary form of the positive integer n has (its Hamming weight).

  • 1 <= n <= 2³¹ − 1

Example: 11 (1011) → 3. 128 → 1. 2147483645 → 30.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
2147483647 31 The most 1 bits possible: the worst case for Approach 3 (31 rounds).
1073741824 (2³⁰) 1 One high bit: Approach 2 still shifts 31 times (1.5 µs in Python), Approach 3 needs 1 round (0.16 µs).
11 3 In Java, if (n & 1 == 1) doesn't compile: == runs before &. Write (n & 1) == 1.

Approach 1: Test All 32 Bits

For i from 0 to 31, (n >> i) & 1 is bit i. Add them up.

  • Always 32 rounds, whatever n is.
Time O(1) (32 rounds) Space O(1)

Average per call over 20,006 inputs: Python 1.6 µs, Java 0.05 µs, C++ 0.02 µs.

Approach 2: Shift Until Zero

Add n & 1, shift n right, and stop when n is 0. The loop ends right after the highest 1 bit.

  • Fast for small numbers, still up to 31 rounds for big ones.
  • In Java use >>>: with >>, a negative number would never reach 0.
Time O(log n) Space O(1)

Average per call: Python 1.6 µs, Java 0.06 µs, C++ 0.04 µs. Random inputs are mostly large, so it saves little over Approach 1.

Approach 3: Clear the Lowest 1 (Brian Kernighan) Optimal

Subtracting 1 flips the lowest 1 bit to 0 and every 0 below it to 1. So n & (n − 1) keeps everything above that bit and clears the bit itself. Count how many times you can do this before n is 0.

  • Rounds = number of 1 bits, so sparse numbers finish almost at once.
  • The same trick checks for a power of two: n & (n − 1) == 0.
Time O(number of 1 bits) Space O(1)

Average per call: Python 0.98 µs, Java 0.06 µs, C++ 0.03 µs. On 2147483647 it's no faster (31 rounds, 1.9 µs in Python).

In practice Built-ins

Every language has a popcount: bin(n).count("1") or n.bit_count() (Python 3.10+), __builtin_popcount or C++20's std::popcount, and Java's Integer.bitCount. Many CPUs count bits in a single instruction.

Time O(1) Space O(1)

Should pass on LeetCode. Python's version averaged 0.24 µs, 4 times faster than Approach 3, because the counting happens in C.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Test All 32 Bits (n >> i) & 1 for each i O(1) O(1) Always 32 rounds
Shift Until Zero Lowest bit, then shift O(log n) O(1) Stops after the highest 1
Clear the Lowest 1 n &= n − 1 O(ones) O(1) Expected answer
268. Missing Number Easy Bit Manipulation Math Array
Key idea: XOR all the indexes 0..n and all the values together. Every number that's present shows up twice (once as an index, once as a value) and cancels, since x ^ x = 0. The missing number is what's left. O(n) time, O(1) space. The sum 0 + 1 + … + n minus the actual sum works the same way.

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

nums holds n different numbers from the range 0..n. Exactly one is missing. Return it.

  • 1 <= n <= 10⁴, all values different

Example: [3,0,1] → 2. [0,1] → 2. [9,6,4,2,3,5,7,0,1] → 8.

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
[0] 1 The missing number is n itself. The sorted scan without a final return n found no gap; wrong on 503 of 3007 tests.
[1] 0 0 is missing: check from 0, not 1.
[0,1] 2 The range is 0..n, so n = 2 counts.

Approach 1: Sort

After sorting, index i should hold i. The first index that doesn't is the answer; if every one does, the answer is n.

Time O(n log n) Space O(1) in place (O(n) for Python's sorted)

10⁴ values: Python 1.1 ms, Java 0.69 ms, C++ 0.17 ms, the slowest in every language.

Approach 2: Mark What's There

Mark every value as seen, then check 0, 1, …, n for the first one that isn't. The values are at most n, so C++ and Java use an array of n + 1 flags instead of a hash set.

Time O(n) Space O(n)

10⁴ values: Python 0.43 ms, Java 47 µs, C++ 8.7 µs.

Approach 3: XOR Optimal

Start with res = n (the one index with no slot). For each i, do res ^= i ^ nums[i]. Pairs cancel, and the missing number remains.

  • XOR can't overflow; a sum can in languages with fixed-size ints (here n ≤ 10⁴ keeps the sum small, so both work).
Time O(n) Space O(1)

10⁴ values: Python 0.40 ms, Java 27 µs, C++ 4.0 µs, the fastest in C++ and Java.

In practice Built-ins

In Python, Gauss's formula with sum: n(n + 1)/2 − sum(nums). Python ints don't overflow.

Time O(n) Space O(1)

Should pass on LeetCode: 34 µs for 10⁴ values, 12 times faster than the XOR loop in Python, because sum runs in C.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Sort First index i not holding i O(n log n) O(1) Don't forget n
Mark What's There Flags for 0..n O(n) O(n) Simple to explain
XOR Pairs cancel O(n) O(1) Expected answer
338. Counting Bits Easy Bit Manipulation Dynamic Programming
Key idea: i >> 1 is i without its last bit. It's smaller, so its count is already known: ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). One step per number, O(n).

Problem View on LeetCode (opens in a new tab) ↗

Return an array ans of length n + 1 where ans[i] is the number of 1 bits in i.

  • 0 <= n <= 10⁵
  • Follow-up: do it in O(n) without a built-in popcount.

Example: n = 2 → [0,1,1]. n = 5 → [0,1,1,2,1,2].

Edge cases

Try these against your solution before reading the approaches.

Input Expected Why it's tricky
n = 0 [0] The array still has one entry.
n = 3 [0,1,1,2] ans[i >> 1] + i & 1 without brackets means (ans[i >> 1] + i) & 1, because + comes before &. It gave [0,1,1,0], and was wrong for 297 of the 300 values of n tried.

Approach 1: Count Each Number

For every i, clear its lowest 1 with x & (x − 1) until it's 0, counting the rounds (as in 191. Number of 1 Bits).

  • Nothing is reused between numbers.
Time O(n log n) Space O(1) besides the answer

n = 10⁵, average of 60 runs: Python 40 ms, Java 0.44 ms, C++ 0.063 ms.

Approach 2: DP on the Lowest 1

i & (i − 1) is i with its lowest 1 cleared. It's smaller, so its count is known, and it has exactly one 1 less: ans[i] = ans[i & (i − 1)] + 1.

  • O(n) and short.
Time O(n) Space O(1) besides the answer

n = 10⁵: Python 5.2 ms, Java 0.087 ms, C++ 0.23 ms. In C++ that's slower than Approach 1. Probably because for every odd i, i & (i − 1) is i − 1: each step waits for the value the step before just wrote.

Approach 3: DP on the Last Bit Optimal

i >> 1 drops the last bit, so ans[i] = ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1). Odd numbers have one more 1 than half of them; even numbers have the same.

  • It reads ans[i / 2], written long ago, so steps don't wait on each other.
Time O(n) Space O(1) besides the answer

n = 10⁵: Python 5.4 ms, Java 0.069 ms, C++ 0.039 ms. Fastest in C++ (5.8 times Approach 2) and Java; in Python, 5% behind Approach 2.

In practice Built-ins

Call a popcount on each number: i.bit_count() (Python 3.10+), __builtin_popcount or C++20's std::popcount, Java's Integer.bitCount. It doesn't meet the follow-up, but it's what you'd write.

Time O(n) Space O(1) besides the answer

n = 10⁵: Python 2.3 ms (2.3 times faster than Approach 3), C++ 0.018 ms (2.2 times faster). Java 0.21 ms, 3 times slower than Approach 3 here.

Comparison

Approach Technique Time Space Notes
Count Each Number Clear the lowest 1, repeat O(n log n) O(1) 40 ms in Python
DP on the Lowest 1 ans[i & (i − 1)] + 1 O(n) O(1) Slow in C++
DP on the Last Bit ans[i >> 1] + (i & 1) O(n) O(1) Expected answer
